speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) asked a question about the Korean armistice negotiations, to which I shall now reply.
There is no foundation to the suggestion that the negotiators for the United Nations command may withdraw from ithe truce talks. The negotiators for the United Nations command have put forward a package proposal for the solution of outstanding differences over the armistice. The communist negotiators have subjected the United States officers who are acting for the United Nations command to considerable abuse to serve the ends of their own propaganda and the United Nations negotiators have therefore recently taken the reasonable position that the main sessions might well be recessed from time to time until the communists are ready to make proposals which are constructive, not merely abusive.
Nevertheless it is the view of the Canadian government, and this is shared by other governments concerned, that if the armistice talks are finally broken off, that should be clearly the responsibility of the communists. In saying this I do not mean to suggest that we are not conscious of the gravity of the situation in Korea because of the build-up of communist military forces in recent months.
The negotiation of a military armistice has, by agreement, been entrusted to military officers on both sides. In accordance with the general outline of a plan for settling the Korean war contained in the supplementary report of the cease-fire group which was approved by the political committee of the general assembly of the United Nations on January 13, 1951, political discussions as such are not to be held until an armistice has been arranged and the fighting has ceased. I admit that the political content of these armistice discussions has now become significant. Whether, however, the machinery on the United Nations side for conducting them should be modified, or whether, indeed, an effort should be made to move the discussions from Korea itself, is another question on which I would not wish to express any opinion at this time.

May I ask this supplementary question: I notice that Right Hon. Mr. Eden is to issue a white paper regarding the position in South Korea, particularly with regard to the activities of Mr. Syngman Rhee. Would

the minister inform us as to the views of the Canadian government in regard to these matters. He need not do so today, necessarily.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose last night I was discussing the problem of the 65-year-old people who, through no fault of their own, have been forced to retire on inadequate pensions, and in many cases without any pension whatsoever. Then there is the related problem concerning those people who, having reached the age of 35 without having established themselves in permanent employment, find they are not eligible for most of the positions in the larger industries where permanent employment could be had, or in various governmental departments.

It is my view that the government could lead the way in this regard by permitting those who are qualified to take civil service examinations, regardless of age, provided always that they are suitable for the positions offered. Only those who have had service with branches of the armed forces are eligible after reaching the age of 35. Then, in industry the unskilled workman, if he is over that age, finds that his position is prejudiced. If he is skilled he may find that in some industries he may obtain permanent employment. I believe the government should take the lead in finding a solution to this problem. The national advisory council in the Department of Labour, which was set up two years ago, could study the matter. Failing that, I suggest the committee on industrial relations might be given the task.
I have one further point to bring to the attention of the minister, although it may not deal specifically with his department. It has direct reference to the productive capacity of the nation, and I feel that representations made by the minister to the Minister of Finance might be influential in bringing about a solution to this problem, which I discussed on another occasion.
During the debate on the budget last year I made reference to the necessity for tax relief in respect of earnings made through an incentive system in excess of regular pay. As recently as yesterday the Minister of Finance agreed that the answer to our heavy taxation problem, and to the maintenance of our standard of living, lies in the productive effort of the nation. Many industries have adopted the incentive system. I am not one who will say I believe that employees are not turning in a fair day's work for a fair day's pay. It is realized that many labour unions are in complete agreement with the idea of an incentive system.
When incentive systems have been established it has been found that over-all production has been increased as much as 30 to 50 per cent, not necessarily because of harder work by the workers but because there has been a better adaptation of the facilities at hand, and the initiative of the various workmen has thus been increased. In some cases the increased production and earnings has been as high as 100 per cent.
However, we find that when a workman increases his production with a consequent increase in his earnings, the income tax takes a large portion of those extra earnings thereby defeating the very purpose for which the incentive system was established. The Department of Finance has established an incentive system in connection with the investment of capital because there is no tax
Supply-Labour
on capital gains. It is felt that a capital gains tax would curtail capital expansion, which no doubt is true, and apparently it has been thought inadvisable to increase the tax on corporations.
I feel that labour should be considered a partner in industry who is willing to invest the excess of labour over the normal amount required. That being so, labour should be treated similarly to the way capital is treated.
Those are the two problems I wished to raise. They may not be completely related, but they are related because of the necessity of increased production not only to provide for the war effort we are presently putting forth but to ensure the financing of our very extensive social program.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that the Minister of Labour would think me remiss in my duty if I did not say something on this first item in his estimates. I want to assure him that I am not going to be critical of what has been done by his department as I am more concerned about the things that have not been done but which I think should be done. I make these suggestions so that the minister, his genial parliamentary assistant and others in the department may read them. If they consider they have merit then I know something may be done about them in the future.
I have always considered the Department of Labour to be one of the most important departments of government. That department has serious and broad responsibilities. For example, they must handle the whole manpower problem so that national defence may get sufficient people for the different services and so that the Department of Defence Production may have the required technical personnel and general labour. They also have a lot to do with the Department of Agriculture because when harvesting time rolls around it is the responsibility of the Department of Labour to find the necessary labour to get in the harvest.
While many members in the house and many people outside the house look upon the Department of Labour as being a department that simply looks after strikes, disputes and so forth, actually this department plans many of the activities of the other departments, with the possible exception of the Department of Finance. I suppose the financial people are careful that you do not get into their realm to any extent.
In dealing with the ramifications and the responsibilities of the Department of Labour I must say that I am not completely satisfied with the job which has been done in one

Supply-Labour
or two fields. I am not satisfied with the job the manpower committee is doing. When that committee was set up about two years ago I said that I did not think it was broad enough because its personnel was being selected largely from the ivory towers of Ottawa. If that committee was to be realistic and in a position to make an appraisal of the manpower problems facing industry across the country, industrial councils should have been set up formed of representatives of the major industries in the country, of men who could talk from the standpoint of industry, who had personal contact with the workers in that particular industry. Those men could meet with the Department of Labour and discuss a particular industry from personal knowledge and be able to guide the department in its labour problems as well as the vocational training program.
I notice that the cost of running this committee last year was $57,000, but an amount of around $107,000 is being asked for this year. I realize that most of this money is required for clerical work, publications and so forth, but it is almost double the previous vote. Apparently the personnel of the committee is exactly as it was when it was formed.
I leave that point with the committee. If you are going to get in touch with those who really represent the workers in industry across the country you must have on that committee those who are closer to the problem than the present members. I am not saying anything about their personal qualifications but I do submit that it is necessary to have on that committee those who are more closely associated with industry and the people employed therein.
My second point is that I am not completely satisfied with the vocational training program because it has not produced very much. The estimates indicate that last year we spent approximately $8,700,000 to bring people to this country, many of them being farm labour. The minister indicated in his statement last night that we have had to bring in skilled labour, and will still have to bring them in. That adds up to the fact that our vocational training or apprenticeship plans have not been pushed as realistically as they should have been.
I have in my hand a press clipping dealing with this subject. It is dated May 24 and refers to the fact that the Department of Labour had convened a representative gathering in Ottawa on that date. The purpose of the gathering was to bring people together from the unions and industry to ascertain if there was not some way that the apprenticeship program to train personnel for industry could be stepped up. I do not know
[Mr. Gillis.l
what happened, but the statement indicates that industry will not sponsor such a program; the unions do not encourage it and it is difficult to interest apprentices. The statement indicates that actually nothing was done. Ideas were exchanged but nothing concrete came out of the conference and it was indicated that the benefits, if any, would not be noticeable for at least a year.
I do not think that is good enough. I do not think we are going to find a solution to the problem of securing more apprentices in conferences at Ottawa. I do not think we are going to find it through spending $8 million odd to bring people into the country. We are stuck so far as the skilled trades are concerned because over the years we have neglected to push the necessary vocational training program. I am not trying to saddle the present administration of the Department of Labour with the problem because it has been neglected for a long time. It is one that is not going to be overcome overnight but a start must be made.
To begin with, the matter of vocational training is a provincial responsibility. In the first place the provincial governments have to be sold the idea, and it has to be proved to them that they must do something about it. Second, instead of depending on industry to do something about it or the unions to push it, it is my opinion that what must be done is to find the necessary finances to build vocational training schools. I think the crux of the problem in the provinces, and particularly in the maritimes, is that they have not the necessary funds to provide schools. If you have not got the funds to provide schools and to pay the trained personnel necessary to staff them then you are not going to do anything about it. Industry is not responsible and neither are the unions. In my opinion the federal Department of Labour does not have the authority to push a vocational training program as they should be able to.
There is an item of approximately $2 million in the estimates this year to provide assistance by way of grants to the provinces to construct vocational schools. Under our present set-up the problem goes deeper than the provincial governments. I know that for years in my part of the country there has been talk of building a vocational school in the city of Sydney. I know that in at least two election campaigns the provincial government said that such a school would be built in the city of Sydney, but over the years all that has ever been done about it is that the provincial government, I suppose as the result of the grant from the federal government, decided that they would put up a certain amount of money to build that school.

Each municipality was then called upon to provide its share of the cost of the school. The federal grant was available, and I suppose the province could find its share of what it would cost to build that school, but many of the municipalities could not put up the necessary funds and for that reason the school was not built. Unless you can get the money to build such schools and staff them there will be no progress so far as any vocational training scheme is concerned. In my opinion the lack of funds on the part of the municipalities is the stumbling block in our whole apprenticeship training program.
It is a serious and pressing problem because, as was pointed out by the committee which was convened on the 24th of May, the older skilled men are dying and the young fellows are not coming up to replace them. They pointed out that while industry has expanded tremendously in the last few years the training programs necessary to provide men to operate the complicated machines of industry today were not in existence. Instead of overcoming the problem we are actually building up a new problem for the federal Department of Labour which has to deal with it. Whether or not they have the authority to provide schools they have to cope with the manpower problem. At the present time we are being compelled to import trained personnel from outside this country. I think that it is a very serious matter because it involves our defence production program, our national defence program and our whole industrial set-up. I think it is serious enough for the federal government to get in touch with the provinces and ascertain what they are prepared to do as soon as possible for the purpose of providing schools.
I am sure if you can get buildings designed to do that job erected in any section of this country you will not have any difficulty in getting apprentices. However, the municipalities have got to be relieved of the responsibility of putting up a certain amount of money as their share because they cannot afford it. The financial problem must be recognized. If we had spent $8 million last year in grants to establish such schools rather than to bring people into the country I think that we might have had a set-up for an apprenticeship training scheme throughout the country. I leave that thought with the minister because it is a very serious matter. It is a must and is in the best interests of the people of Canada.
I have been of the opinion since 1945 that we place too much emphasis on university training and far too little on vocational training and fitting the men of the future to run the machines of the future in our industrial set-up. There must be some new thinking on the problem because we are always going to
Supply-Labour
have hewers of wood and drawers of water. Everybody cannot go around with long hair looking down at the ground in a serious manner. There still have to be producers, and I believe if there is more emphasis on a vocational training scheme in the future and the building of such schools you will have no trouble in staffing them and not very much trouble in getting apprentices if the problem is tackled on that basis.
There is another matter about which I want to say a few words. I refer to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I know there are amendments to the act before the house at the present time in the form of a bill. What I have to say does not concern the bill but has to do with regulation 5A and the position of married women under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I think that married women are being seriously discriminated against under that particular section. I had a case which I followed right along the line. I thought that when we amended the act last year we had softened it a little bit and that there would be no trouble for a married woman who complied with the sensible requirements of the act. Unfortunately, however, after we write an act and set it out so that it looks fine somebody sits down behind the scenes and writes regulations. You may have a nice looking paragraph in the act that says that this shall be done under given circumstances but somebody writes about thirty regulations to prevent everything you put in the act happening. That is pretty much the way I look at regulation 5A. I thought all a married woman had to do was to work ninety days in insurable employment after she married to be qualified for unemployment insurance.
It does not work like that. I had brought to my attention the case of a little girl. She got married, and intended to continue working after marriage. She did not even take time off to get married. She used her vacation period for that purpose. She went back to work with her previous employer and carried on for 93 or 96 days, or some period like that; at any rate it was over the statutory requirement. Then nature played a trick on her, and she was in the position that she just could not carry on with that work. Her employer noticed that she had slowed up a bit in her work and he told her so. He laid the little girl off and hired someone else in her place. Naturally she thought she was entitled to unemployment insurance.
The situation is not bad in an industrial section that is highly unionized, where one can get advice or can hand one's problem over to the union; but this girl is living out in a rural section. She is not close

Supply-Labour
to offices. But immediately she was laid off she reported for work and continued to report for work. She was advised by the manager of the Sydney office that she was not entitled to unemployment insurance. She could not understand why not. She came down to see me and I went over the case with her. Having regard to the amendment that we had made to the act, I thought that the girl was in the clear. She is laid off. She has complied with the statute. She has worked 93 or 96 days. I called up the manager of the office and he said, "Oh, no; you forget the regulations." I said, "I have never yet seen the regulations." The girl appealed her case. I was her solicitor. I went before the board of referees. I argued the case for her and at least succeeded in splitting the board. One chap on the board said I was right; the other two said I was wrong. In any event, they not only disallowed her claim but they penalized that woman by debarring her from unemployment insurance for the next two years.
I was not satisfied with that judgment. In view of the fact that the board had disagreed on the matter, I said, "O.K.; we will take it the next step." I was sure I would get justice from a learned judge in Ottawa, so we took the matter to the umpire. The umpire is the final court of appeal. The evidence was all set out. The umpire decided that the woman was not entitled to unemployment insurance, and confirmed the penalty that was provided, namely, that she lose her unemployment insurance for the next two years.
In my opinion the thing was absolutely crazy. I have read the evidence. I have a copy of it oni my desk here. If the minister or anyone else in this committee who has any idea of fair play would take that case and read it over, and find out how an adverse decision could be handed down, I should be glad to be informed. I cannot understand it, because everything the act asked for or compelled her to do, she did. The fact that someone behind the scenes wrote a regulation with regard to a married woman in a certain condition is no reason why unemployment insurance should not be paid to her. That woman was laid off. She might have worked for seven or eight months longer. She reported for work every day, and to the best of my knowledge, is still doing so.
That case is, of course, closed. That girl is not going to get her unemployment insurance. For my part, I think that it is a rank miscarriage of justice. That girl paid for unemployment insurance for five years. After doing that her insurance is refused her. I believe she would be justified in suing the unemployment insurance commission for
[Mr. Gillis.I
the return of the money she paid in because she certainly was not given the protection for which she insured herself.
I suggest to the minister that someone should take a look at that regulation 5A, particularly those regulations, and just see how impossible it is, under the regulations, for a married woman to qualify for unemployment insurance. If we are going to accept married women as insurable, then we should see to it that they at least get the same protection in the same way as the man who pays in to the unemployment insurance fund, and that they are accorded as liberal an interpretation of the act. If we are not going to do that, we should cut them off altogether, not take their money under false pretences and deny them the protection that they think they are paying for while they are paying into the unemployment insurance fund.
That is not a criticism, may I say to the minister; that is a plea, on the basis of a miscarriage of justice, that he should take a look at the regulations under the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would also say that, in selecting the court of referees, which is the local court of appeal, you should be careful to select men who really understand the act and its purpose, and who are young enough to form judgments that are a little bit more flexible than some of the ones I have seen. For example

and I am not going to say where you may find this type of people- to take an old man who was employed in an official capacity for years in an industry and who, when he reaches the point where he is pensioned off, is 75 or 80 years of age, and to put him on a board to give judgments in disputes of that kind on modern, up-to-date legislation is a procedure that I think is wrong. I think you can get people whose minds are a little bit more flexible than that. I think if you get on the local board of referees the right kind of people, you will have little reason to send any cases to the umpire in Ottawa. I know that my first experience in trying to handle the problem through that machinery left much to be desired.
There is another subject on which I should like to say a few words, Mr. Chairman; I refer to the construction strike at present causing trouble in the Halifax area. The reason I mention the matter here is that I am informed that most of the projects where the wage dispute has taken place are government contracts. I was of the opinion that as to all government contracts of any size, when they were let, the Department of Labour generally attached to them a wage

schedule that was fair and reasonable in comparison with the rates that prevailed in the district concerned.
I do not know what the set-up is in the city of Halifax with regard to carpenters' unions and so forth; but my information is that, having regard to the dispute that is going on there at the present time, the carpenters are badly underpaid in comparison with the general wage rates in that industry. They also make the observation that since 1949 they have received an adjustment of only 10 cents per hour in their wage rates across the board. They have had no adjustment since that time.
In most of the industries-and I think this is true in most of the building trades as well-there has been a much more substantial adjustment than that in wage rates on a national scale. I know that this problem is one for the department of labour in the city of Halifax. It is their responsibility. But at the same time if it is true that most of the projects where the disputes arise are federal government projects, I think the Minister of Labour or some of his conciliation officers from here should take a look at the situation and should at least bring the wage rates in that area, in the building industry, into line with those that prevail on a national scale. I find it hard to understand why there is difficulty in the building trades, because there has been little in the past. It is the one industry in Canada which has a national industrial council that meets with the Department of Labour from time to time and irons out the difficulties that may exist in the building trades. It has worked very well in the past, so there must be some lack of co-ordination with the national industry in this particular case. In any event, I am suggesting that the minister might look at that to see to what extent government contracts are involved in that wage dispute, and in that way he may be able to help the whole situation in that area.
There is another thing about which I was rather disappointed. Last session the Minister of Labour introduced a bill to amend the Annuities Act. We had the pleasure of examining that bill in a committee under the chairmanship of the member for Edmonton East. After the introduction of the bill I was not surprised to find that the insurance companies put on quite a lobby around the house, and sent many very vocal witnesses to the committee who complained that the bill was unfair competition. I was not very much concerned about their arguments, because I have always felt the Annuities Act was a yardstick, set up by the government, by which one could measure the rates
Supply-Labour
of the old line companies. In my opinion it was the only stabilizing factor in the whole insurance field.
I was convinced that, without the Annuities Act, we would have been a good many years establishing our group insurance plans. This act laid the basis for those group insurance plans, and to a large extent set the actuarial basis which enabled fair and reasonable rates to be established. After much wrangling the bill was laid to one side. I hope that as soon as the minister can get around to it that act will be reintroduced. The amendments merely brought the act into line with the old companies. They provided for a cash surrender value, and stepped up the amount by another few hundred dollars. This act does not provide unfair competition, but it is a yardstick that will perhaps hold the other companies' rates in line, because in all forms of insurance in this country, life, property and car insurance, the rates have skyrocketed within a short space of time. I believe that legislation such as the Annuities Act is desirable in the public interest, and should be enacted as soon as we can possibly do it.
I am going to conclude, Mr. Chairman, by again mentioning to the minister something that I have mentioned on several other occasions. I think the department should give consideration to designating certain industries in this country as national industries. I am thinking of industries that are basic to our economy. In this event the federal government would have some say when trouble arose. I believe that coal, steel, packing house and communications are the important industries. We had a good demonstration of what happens from province to province when an industry like the packing house industry gets tied up on a national scale. The labour department in Ottawa found itself in the position of being unable to do anything except offer advice, because the responsibility rested with each province despite the fact it was a national strike that was affecting the food supplies of the people of Canada. It was impossible to get the nine provinces together to try to get some unanimity of interest as to how the matter should be handled as between the provinces. In these difficult times in which we are living it is a shortsighted policy to leave the federal government in a position of being unable to act when industries that are basic to our economy and to our whole defence project may be tied up by strikes.
The minister may say that the department might be able to do something under the Emergency Powers Act which we extended a few days ago. I noticed that, despite the fact that act existed during the packing house strike, it was not invoked; nothing was done about it. We have a national labour code

Supply-Labour
under which come the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the harbours board and shipping that may be engaged in interprovincial trade. I believe that we should include within the jurisdiction of this code the industries which I have mentioned, which are national in scope and are equally important from the standpoint of what might happen in an emergency. In the event of trouble, the adjustment of wages and that kind of thing, or in the prevention of trouble which is more important than untangling a mess, I believe that the federal government is in a much better position to act than any of the provincial governments. The federal department has an excellent conciliation service with trained personnel who are able to handle these situations much better than the average provincial set-up.
I know that so far as I am concerned I have been of the opinion for a good many years that the mining industry should be a national industry. I would much rather come here to find the solution to a problem than I would go to provincial departments, because they are wrapped up rather tightly with the industrialist himself, and it is difficult to get any thinking that is not warped and biased. A national coal board has been set up with jurisdiction in allocating financial assistance to this industry. I am definitely of the opinion that the coal mining industry should be a national industry, and so should steel, packing house and communications. They should be placed under the national labour code so that if at any time it appeared as if something was developing in any of those industries that might tie them up, the labour department in Ottawa would be in a position to act instead of having to wire the provincial governments in order to get some decision. In the final analysis, it is nearly impossible to get any unanimity amongst them.
I am just making these rambling remarks, Mr. Speaker, to provoke some thought on the part of the minister, and perhaps he may do something about them in the future.

I always appreciate the logic with which the member for Cape Breton South attacks the problem before us. This being Friday the 13th, Mr. Chairman, in deference to my superstitious Irish ancestors I am wondering just how I should attack the problem before me. I want to assure the minister, however, that I am not going to throw any horse shoes at him or anything like that. In fact, I intend to be rather kind to him today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In an Irish way.

I have heard of the fellow who said he got just what he

expected, and a friend of his said, "Well, you ought to be thankful you did not get what you deserved." I have in my hand a volume which I hope the minister does not think is my notes. Perhaps I should have written to the minister about it. I want to take a moment to deal with the telephone directory of the city of London and district. Believe it or not, it is almost impossible to find the Department of Labour with the other offices of the government of Canada. If you want to find national employment you find it wedged in between National Dry and National Grocers. Unemployment insurance is pretty nearly the last thing in the book. Under the title "Government of Canada" there is a labour department, but no national employment and no unemployment insurance. The people there who want to get these offices look in the book for Joseph P. Ryan. They know who he is. I hope that will be taken care of.
I have given some thought to this problem. It is a problem that is troubling the minds of most Canadians. I do not need to mention what it is. Across the line there is a steel strike. The hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned the strike in the construction industry in the maritimes. Every time there is a strike certain people are perturbed; industry is thrown out of kilter and losses ensue. Our industrial picture is changing. If you go back a hundred years you find that most of the industries were family concerns, and the owners knew all their employees. If there were difficulties they were talked over; if someone was sick or in difficulties he was taken care of. In our industrial development management and labour have gone farther apart. Then, in some instances organizers, and men who have sought to create differences between labour and management, have profited thereby.
With that thought in mind and with my tongue in my cheek I have risen today to try to offer a little constructive criticism, as I see it, on some of the things that might be done and that are being done around about us.
Just in passing I want to mention that probably no group in the country has more to lose by governments taking over all industry, as is done in the socialist countries where the individual loses his liberty, than labour. I mention this because of the statement of William Green, president of the American Federation of Labour, as follows:
Whenever organized labour has surrendered its freedom by opposing the free enterprise system.

the slavery of despotism has become entrenched or has established strongholds that threaten all freedom.
I hear from time to time some hon. members to the left decrying the free enterprise system. I want them to look around the world and they will see that wherever there is a high standard of living they will find that it is the free enterprise system that has built it. To maintain that, I am wondering how we can approach this problem of industrial strife. I do not attach blame to labour alone or to industry alone, but I do know that everyone in the country suffers because of it.
I have some figures that I want to introduce later to highlight that, to point out that labour loses wages when industry loses business, and people generally lose things because of it, and supporting industries are forced to close because of the lay-off of their suppliers. In the long run really no one has gained. More parties are involved than just labour and industry. It is similar to what happened in the last war. It was not the armed forces principally that suffered so much as the innocent bystanders, the civilians, the women and children; and that often happens when industrial strife occurs. The long-suffering public is often the ones that are injured.
Just in that connection I have a little table that struck me as rather interesting. It is taken from the dominion bureau of statistics, and it shows labour's per cent of the production over a period of years. In 1890 the percentage of the total product that labour made was 21-4. In 1939 they had lost a little ground. The figure was 21-2 per cent; and in 1948, which is the last figure that I could get, 20 [DOT] 3 per cent went to labour. Where did it go? During that period-and I can give the figures only for 1929-that is the purchasing power that labour had gained. In other words they did not gain a great deal from industry. In fact, with all the movement that has gone on during those many years, the percentage that they obtained from the industry with which they were engaged decreased. In other words, their gains were made at the expense of groups that were not so well organized. I am going to mention two or three of them.
In 1929 an hour's work bought 6-4 pounds of bread. Today it will buy 10 pounds. We seem to think that meat is dear, but in 1929, strange as it may seem, an hour's labour bought 1-2 pounds; today it buys 1-5 pounds. Back in 1929 an hour's labour would buy only a pound of butter; in 1951 it bought almost two pounds, to be exact, 1 [DOT] 9 pounds. In 1929 an hour's labour bought only 1-1
Supply-Labour
dozen eggs; today it buys 2-5 dozen. I just put these figures on the record to show that gains have been made but they are not always obtained from the ones that we have thought they were obtained from.
I do not think anyone will question this statement. It has long been my contention that the best interests of labour and management are served when they work together as a team and not as one group fighting or opposing another. Therefore any developments that the minister might bring in that will help to bring industry and labour closer together will certainly be to the best interests of all Canadians.
While I am on the question of strikes and losses incurred, may I say that I hold in my hand two of the publications of the Department of Labour dealing with strikes or lockouts in Canada during 1950. During 1950, 1,389,039 man days were lost because of strikes and lockouts. This does not take into consideration the supplying industries that sold to companies that were on strike.
In the first three months of 1952 we have already lost 188,325 man days. It has also been demonstrated that subversive groups are striving, and have been striving, to get control of many of the labour movements. I need only mention the affair at Valleyfield and Kent Rowley to highlight what I mean. I should say, in the same breath, that it is to the everlasting credit of labour that, by democratic means, they are routing out many of these subversive workers in the unions.
There is another thing we pass by a little too lightly, and that is that we are inclined to condone damage to private property or to company property. The labourer would certainly be incensed-so would I and so would any other individual-if, during a strike, attacks were made on his home, and damage done. The damage to plants owned by corporations or companies while a strike is in progress is a loss to everyone, and constitutes a regrettable phase of our industrial relations at the moment.
Not so long ago Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, very wisely said in answer to demands for compulsory arbitration that he would have no part of compulsory arbitration. This is an indication that a large number of people in the country are seeking a way to stall strikes. If serious strikes occur, greater pressure would be brought to bear for compulsory arbitration, but I am one of those who hope that this can be avoided. No doubt nothing suits communists and their fellow travellers better than industrial strife. It is high time more thought was devoted to this problem, and more action taken by all those who are concerned.

Supply-Labour
While I do not offer this as a cure-all or a complete solution, I think steps could be taken to improve the understanding between labour and management in industry. This would be at least an approach to the problem. I have been giving some study to profitsharing industries in the United States and Canada, and in doing so I have come across what, to my mind, are some startling figures, and worth-while results. While I shall not read the whole of it, I would refer to an article in the Reader's Digest written by Walter Cenerazzo, national president of the American watchworkers union. It states, in part:
Nowhere in the world is capitalism operated as in the United States and Canada. Nowhere else is there a virile labour movement dedicated to work within the framework of corporate enterprise. In all other countries the labour movement is a political movement trying to obtain all reforms by legislation. This has become the tendency even on this side of the Atlantic. Our sound trade unionists disagree with a political labour movement, feeling that the best gains can be obtained for the workers at the bargaining table with the employer.
In North America there are no longer numbers of very rich-and we are striving to eliminate the very poor. We are all middle-class, whether we are the president of the bank or the janitor who works for the bank. We all desire a home, an automobile, education for our children and a high standard of living. That is why a virile labour movement must be kept free and democratic in our society.
To me this means investor, management and labour working together for these objectives.
That is what the president of one of the labour organizations in the United States has to say about our present set-up. The idea of profit sharing is really democracy in labour. The few remarks I shall make in this connection are based upon actual experiences of industries that have introduced one or more of the profit-sharing plans into the operation of their companies. At this point I would quote Mr. P. M. Richards:
Free enterprise is doomed unless employees are given partnership by means of the profit-sharing system, says William Loeb, publisher of the Manchester (New Hampshire) Times-Union and chairman of the council of profit-sharing industries.
And later:
In this connection. Mr. Loeb warned that in sharing profits, business must see that the share given to labour is commensurate with the effort labour has put into making that profit; experience shows that the more generous the profit-sharing plan, the more will productivity rise. But it is definitely not a case of "something for nothing," since the workers must do their part to make profits before they can share them.
Profit sharing is any procedure under which an employer pays all employees special immediate or deferred payments based not only upon individual but upon group performance, and also upon the prosperity of the company. In our free democratic way of life this allows the individual to make his

greatest contribution to the wealth of the community, the production of goods and services. Profit sharing is an incentive to do just this.
It would seem inevitable that with a greater degree of profit sharing would come the steadying or stabilizing of our economy. It would seem, further, that when partnership between labour and industry can be achieved by this plan, industrial strife will be superseded by industrial partnership. Some of the chief results taken from the records of industries that have introduced profit-sharing plans are these: Greater efficiency in the production of goods; cheaper goods; higher pay; fewer strikes; more profits for industry spread over longer periods of time; and the elimination of a large turnover of labour.
It is good psychology and strategy, in a world divided between belief in the sacred rights of the individual as against the overpowering rights of the state, that the individual should be supreme. This is one way in which the individual can be a partner in enterprise.
No doubt this question arises in the minds of hon. members: Are there many firms enjoying this type of labour relations? I must confess I have not been able to secure all the data for Canada, but I am told that the percentage in Canada is comparable with that in the United States. The figures I have been able to secure concerning firms in the United States entering into these profit-sharing agreements apply to one half of one per cent of the business firms in that country, and five per cent of all the corporations. As I have pointed out, this percentage carries through into Canada.
In the United States 1,120 firms each year change over from the old type of management to the process of profit sharing.
The question might be asked whether this plan is applicable to both large and small industries. Sears-Roebuck in the United States have 105,000 employees, and are one of the larger companies which have adopted this plan. Howland and Howland, New York city, have some 14 employees. Apparently it is adaptable to large and small enterprises.
The department of internal revenue in the United States reports that over one-third of the industries which have labour union representation in their plants have adopted profitsharing plans. Labour unions and labour generally are agreed on the benefits from this type of management.
Another question is how much of the profits should be shared. The percentage varies from 5 per cent to 100 per cent, the average being slightly under 20 per cent. Not only do industry and labour have a share in the

gains; all groups in the economy which are able to get a better article at lower price because of efficiency, less lost time, and so on benefit as well. In the United States there is no corporation tax applied on profits set aside for plans of this type; the money is not taxed until it becomes part of a person's income.
Another question is, how many different plans are there. One of the beauties of this system is that a plan can be tailor-made to fit almost any industry. There is no hard and fast rule and practically every industry that has adopted this plan has worked out a plan adapted to its own particular needs.
Such a plan involves sharing, not only money but interest, purposes and efforts. There is another thing that many people forget, that enterprises have losses. The question then arises as to who is going to share such losses. It has been found that in industries which have profit-sharing plans the workers consider themselves as partners and are quite prepared to co-operate with management in order to secure markets and do everything to carry them through a period when ordinarily industries are facing difficult going because of losses suffered through competition.
We should be realistic in our approach to this problem, not only as labour and industry but as a democracy, because the preservation of our way of life is involved. If we have paralysing strikes all over the country we might really be in very serious difficulty, particularly with the world situation as it is and no one knowing when we might be called into armed conflict.
I should like to review for a moment some of the achievements that have been reported by participating industries. There has been a 40 to 100 per cent increase in efficiency; labour turnover, as I mentioned before, has been sharply reduced and in many cases eliminated almost entirely; lateness and absenteeism have been reduced as much as 75 per cent; better care has been taken of equipment and there have been fewer grievances and strikes; tremendous savings have been achieved through better workmanship, greater salvage and reduced rejections.
There are waiting lists of men and women seeking employment in those industries which have adopted profit-sharing plans. Strange as it may seem, although when you analyse it it is not so strange, there has been a reduction in the prices of goods manufactured by companies employing this type of plan. There has been increased home ownership by employees.
It may be asked:	Why do we not hear
more about this? I think the answer is that
Supply-Labour
the industries which have adopted these profit-sharing plans find that they are able to compete in a very competitive market because of less labour trouble and decreased costs. Therefore they are not going to say too much about it. They consider that they are sitting pretty, as it were, compared with their competitors who may be having industrial strikes.
No industry or group can enter into such a scheme without giving it serious thought and study, and I think this is where the department comes in. There should be some central place where information could be obtained. I have before me copies of many of the publications put out by the department and I think without spending any more public money good results along the lines I have indicated could be obtained. Unless there is complete understanding on the part of employees and management I think any plan will be doomed to failure. After all, it is a question of partnership.
The Department of Labour should take a long-range view of this matter and make its plans accordingly. When a strike occurs it becomes the duty of the province to send in an arbitrator or referee, but that is after the fight has begun. That is not the point at which the most good can be done. What I am interested in is preventing these fights, not settling them after they get started.
It is most important that management explain its problems to its employees. It should tell its employees about its markets and its competitors. I cannot think of a better way of improving industrial relations than the adoption of the profit-sharing plan. It is the answer to communism, it is the rounding out of democracy, it is the Christian way of life.
There are certain items in the estimates which have a direct connection with this problem. Item 188 deals with the economics and research branch; item 190 has to do with fair wages, conciliation and industrial disputes; item 193 has to do with the Labour Gazette; item 200 has to do with the national advisory council on manpower, on which we are spending $107,940, and many people wonder what we have to show for that; and then there is item 202, which has to do with educational films. Those items total $1,186,822 and it is my opinion that half of that might well be set aside for the purposes I have mentioned. I hope the minister and his department will go to work on this problem.

Mr. Chairman, my general impression of the minister's department is that they are doing a good job. Inasmuch as

Supply-Labour
they are doing a good job, I believe mention should be made of that fact. When people in the country do a good job, they should be given credit no matter to what party they belong. I see no reason why we should be so partisan as to deny honour where honour is due. However, there are three matters that I think should be brought to the minister's attention by more and more members until something is done about them. I am not the first one in parliament to bring them up but I am one, and I hope there will be a good many more. They do not reflect on the minister at all, or on his department. They require that we do a little breaking of new sod.
The first one has to do with men 45 years of age and over. We know that very definite resistance has developed in many industries against the employment of men who have reached the age of 45. This is a manifest injustice developing in our nation which we must take measures to overcome. Exactly What should be done I am not prepared to say because I have not given the matter sufficient study, but something simply must be done to remove from men and women 45 and over the disadvantage under which they are suffering in the matter of obtaining employment.
The next matter that I think must be given attention at a very early date has to do with people who have reached the age of 65 and over. Not very long ago I was travelling on a train on which the conductor was making his last run. The whole thing was about as sad as a funeral. I have seen very few men more sad than this conductor. He was perfectly capable of carrying on and doing a good job but the age limit had come and he had to be laid off. We will grant that when a man reaches the age of 65 it may not be safe to entrust him with the heavy responsibility of being the conductor of a train, or perhaps of taking the lead in a great many other activities in which human life and property may be endangered, by reason of developing failure to co-ordinate and so forth which is likely to come upon any man after he reaches that age. Nevertheless it is in the interests of the nation that the productive capacity which still remains in many men and women after the age of 65 should be employed to the best advantage.
Unless we make provision for that sort of thing we are obviously not going to get out of our economy its greatest productive achievement. Just what ought to be done again is not easy to prescribe. One hesitates to even make a suggestion for fear he might be misunderstood, but when we reflect upon the use that is being made of human energy in various institutions which I think will
[Mr. Blackmore.l
come to mind, human energy which for one reason or another is more or less taken out of circulation permanently from the economy, it seems quite obvious that it should be possible to design something to enable the country to re-employ people who have reached the age of 65. The government will have to take the lead in this matter because private people cannot very well do it. Therefore I want to bring that matter to the minister's attention with the suggestion, that his department give it the very best thought it is capable of bringing to bear on this subject so that something can be done before we have too much suffering.
As the minister very well knows, we are learning now to feed people better and in various ways to take care of them better so that their expectancy of life is being greatly increased. It is a most doleful thought that a man's life should be extended in length only to be spent in idleness which leads in many cases to decay and unhappiness. These are general considerations that in my opinion apply to the proposition.
There is another matter which was more or less indirectly referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I refer to the taking of an unemployment insurance fee from people when it is a foregone conclusion that they are not going to be able to receive unemployment insurance. I know that the whole unemployment insurance scheme is built up to a certain extent on the fees which are taken from people, and I believe it was designed to take fees from a good many people who would never derive any benefit from unemployment insurance. Let us have it clearly understood, however, that for the government to take a fee from -any ordinary individual for a service which that individual is not going to be able to receive is for the government to be indulging in what is morally unsound. In other words, it amounts to theft. That is a pretty severe word to use but I think one can hardly use a milder term and still express the truth. The instance the hon. member for Cape Breton South gave is a good case in point. It is not necessary to do things like that in an economy like Canada's in order to be able to have unemployment insurance.
I do not propose to enter into a discussion of the whole matter but I think everybody in this house or outside who is realistic in the matter of finance must certainly comprehend that there are ways of obtaining the money without resorting to such a device, and without resorting to such a device as the onerous taxation from which we suffer throughout the economy. It is high time that the government in power in Canada began to consider some of these ways and

means. I register my protest against taking money from people from which they are not going to be able to receive any advantage. Probably the remedy cannot be developed all at once but it is high time that we pushed our prow in the right direction and began working towards the desirable goal.

Mr. Chairman, at this particular time it is appropriate to discuss the past story of the Department of Labour under the federal government. In doing so it takes us back through the regime of Sir Wilfrid Laurier when the department was founded and on through the years of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King who was the first deputy minister of this department and then prime minister. As hon. members know, in his lifetime Prime Minister King took a deep interest in the affairs of the department indirectly when prime minister of the day. It gives me considerable satisfaction to have been in the department myself during the years 1942 to 1944 and to have seen later in the opening days of the regime of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent the department doing fine work and the things for which, in the mind of the founder and its first deputy minister, it was established. I take particular satisfaction in seeing Dr. Arthur MacNamara, its present deputy minister, still in office today and carrying on the notable work which he began when he took over during the years of world war II.
The results of the department in the legal sense have been very great over the years. The Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is a model of its kind and constitutes the first controlled collective bargaining statute in Canada. We can mention the wartime labour code. We all remember the good work of the Hon. Humphrey Mitchell in those days and also of the present deputy minister in producing this model labour code which has served so well that many of the provinces have adopted it as the model for their existing labour relations legislation. The unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service are institutions of which most Canadians are proud. Indeed, we are glad today to see the government increasing the allowance under the unemployment insurance legislation and also shortening the waiting period. These improvements are approved on all sides of the house as I am sure they are welcomed by labour and management.
There is another outstanding piece of legislation, and this is the vocational training legislation which this department has administered so ably to date. Here you have actual proof of Canada's recognition of the need for education of the masses as well as of the
Supply-Labour
classes. This government, from its earliest days, has taken great care as to this training, and it is a matter of increasing importance in these times when we find the necessity for this broad outlook and this balance in the field of education. Most Canadians recognize the need for greater skills on the part of those who do manual work. Our legislation, passed as it was by the present regime early in the days when the depression was concluding, is a statute which has increased the skills of the workers commensurate with the job opportunities which arose when this government came back to office in 1935 before the commencement of world war II. It has been said that Prime Minister King cured job scarcity in Canada during the late thirties, but it can be said too that he also provided educational opportunities for vocational training consistent with the job opportunities which were brought about towards the end of the depression.
Today, under the St. Laurent regime, we have at the helm Canada's lawyer without peer. We all know that he went to work early in the days of his regime on the question of Canada abroad at the bar of public opinion abroad; and we have the North Atlantic pact as a monument to his credit. This North Atlantic pact is undoubtedly a gesture of friendship on the part of the Prime Minister and a monument to him which sets him apart as a world statesman in the British commonwealth. However, at home he has also proven his skill as an advocate on behalf of labour at the bar of public opinion.
I was in the hospital at the time when the outstanding national railway strike centred itself on this parliament and was settled with skill by our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I think that the essence of the skill which he displayed is that he pointed out to labour the necessity, in the national crisis, of compulsory arbitration, at the same time reminding them of the seriousness of the position and expressing the firm hope that resort to it should not happen again unless under extreme conditions of national emergency. To see the way labour trusted him is the thing which makes us sure that he follows truly in the tradition of Laurier, and again in the tradition of King, setting himself apart as one quite capable of adding to the labour laws of the country which are to the credit of the government, and setting himself apart again as a trusted friend of all those who came to us here in this parliament at the time of the national railway strike.
The story of the department in the estimates brought forward by the minister today illustrates to me that the minister has in mind clearly the problem of inflation on the home front in Canada. We have seen the effect of

Supply-Labour
governmental taxes, credit and monetary controls in stemming the tide of inflation. We trust that there is a measure of stability which will last. But we also see, in the legislation of the department, encouragement of production on all sides, which is a good weapon against inflation. There has been encouragement to the ordinary working force by way of these increased benefits in the unemployment insurance legislation. We can point to that legislation as something which will encourage production and also help to stem the tide of inflation. Above all, the increases in the estimates for vocational training stand as something which provides for the youth of Canada opportunities to increase their skill, to increase their production, and to help on the question of inflation.
I note with interest that the minister has been able-and I think it is to his credit- to increase his vocational training estimates as he saw fit in an amount of $375,000 this year for purposes which become apparent as the estimates are examined. It is interesting to note that the record of the government has been extensive in this vocational training field in the post-war period. To date $58,641,625 has been spent on the matter of vocational training in the post-war period down to the last fiscal year now concluded.
It was interesting last evening to listen to the minister as he told about the apprenticeship conference here at the national level. Industry was represented, as were labour, the provinces and his own department. Although the minister is unable to predict-and I think wisely so-the future outcome and the immediate results of the conference, I am sure that these results nevertheless will bear fruit, knowing the minister and the officials he has with him in this matter. I know that at the conference approval was given to the proposals of the conference as to apprenticeship training, not only by management but also by the top figures of the labour organizations; I refer to Mr. A. R. Mosher and Mr. Percy Bengough in this connection.
Naturally labour is going to be concerned about the way in which the policies laid down by the conference are implemented. Labour will not want to see great pools of labour trained in the wrong places and at the wrong time. But I think it is a good sign that labour representatives at the conference endorsed the principles laid down and considered, naturally, providing necessary safeguards. Knowing the department and its reputation for carefully implementing policies of this kind, I think we can rely upon it to do a good piece of work. I think hon. members should encourage the minister, when his supplementary estimates come

before the committee, to further the aims and the findings of the conference.
It came as good news to me when I heard the minister report about the conference, because early in the life of this session I placed on the order paper a resolution which I was able to discuss briefly before the house in another debate. This resolution is on the order paper and, if the chairman will permit me to do so, I will read it so that it may be included in the record of these, my remarks. It reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give early consideration to the making of provision for increased financial assistance for the improvement and extension of vocational training facilities and the training of workers in skilled trades and occupations with a view to providing adequate facilities and opportunities for training workers in all sections of Canada and developing and increasing the skills and numbers of workers in essential trades and occupations in the national interest.
I think this is a worthy resolution, Mr. Chairman. Indeed, I have received from my colleagues on the government side general commendation as to the resolution. I think that members of this chamber on all sides approved the statement of the minister with regard to this matter of vocational training and increasing the apprenticeship side of it. And, too, the people of Canada have shown their need for increased vocational training facilities. I know that because the figures indicate that in the vocational training establishments in 1949-50 there were 179,043 individuals registered, and in the year 1951-52 the enrolment increased to 226,075.
It would be an oversight on my part if before taking my seat I did not indicate to the minister a personal debt to the department in my ordinary duties within the riding of Toronto Rosedale. We have there the Rosedale Liberal Association, which called upon me to take the nomination for my seat in parliament as of the month of April, 1949. At that time it was the policy of that association in the riding to establish there a permanent Liberal committee room on Parliament street. I wish to report to the house that since that time the association has obtained this committee room, with a permanent secretary on duty from 3 to 6 p.m. daily for five days a week. The purpose of the committee room is to serve the residents of the riding in connection with their legal, governmental, social welfare, and other problems which they may bring there for consideration. The practice is to refer the individuals concerned to the appropriate sources which can give them assistance in their needs. In that sense it has been called

a referral bureau, and it has been welcomed by no less than 1,000 people during the period of its operation in the riding.
If the chairman will permit me, I should pay tribute to the national employment service in Toronto for giving all possible assistance to us in our work in the committee room, f mention in particular the sympathetic outlook of those officers in that local office in Toronto in counselling senior citizens in the matter of employment. In the association we believe, and I know the impression has been gained for the most part in the riding, that there is a deep sense of personal interest on the part of the officers and officials of the local national employment office. Further, we believe that the national employment office in Toronto is carrying out the will of the people in the democratic sense, to the end that people have their needs satisfied in so far as is reasonably possible. We thank the minister for the co-operation and service of his officials, and for enabling us to make democracy work better at the riding level. We thank him further for enabling us to keep close to the people where, in my opinion, we who are in public life belong.
As a result of the minister's vocational training program, and the expansion of it, I intend to recommend to the executive of the association that in the future we include a new feature in the service rendered by the committee room. I believe that an opportunity exists for the members of the association, and particularly the executive, to assist the people of Rosedale riding on the question of vocational guidance. I wish to assure the minister that when his new program is well under way we shall endeavour to bring the program to the people of Rosedale riding, so that their needs may be fulfilled and they may obtain the fullest possible benefit from the program.
In closing, I wish to congratulate the minister on the vocational training program, because in my opinion it will produce more skilled workers, more production, better wages, a better standard of living, less inflation, and a better war prevention program in defence of freedom.

Mr. Chairman, I was very glad to learn last night from the minister's remarks that the question of rehabilitation in industry is receiving the government's attention, and to learn also that an advisory council on rehabilitation is to be set up. I believe that is a very good step. I only hope that this advisory council on rehabilitation will be given more opportunity to do good work than has the advisory council on manpower, which was set up with such great hope more than a year and a half ago.
Supply-Labour
The reason I say that about the advisory council on manpower is because the only way you can judge a body and what it does is by the reports of its meetings. I have here a news release sent out by the Department of Labour, reporting on the latest meeting of the advisory council on manpower, held on February 26 last. I have read it very carefully, but I cannot find one reference to any suggestion which was made by any member of the advisory council on manpower. In fact, I cannot find any reference to any member of that council being there, but I am sure they were.
It is a lengthy report, and contains a good many reports which were obviously laid before the advisory council on manpower by the government. In fact, I have studied these various news releases sent out by the Department of Labour when the advisory council on manpower has had its infrequent meetings, and I have yet to find more than one reference to advice being given to the government by a member of the council. That was a short statement of about half a paragraph by Mr. Rhys Sale of the Ford Company of Canada, about a year ago.
I feel that is a very regrettable state of affairs. When the council was set up, the membership appeared to be very worth while. It seems to me unfortunate that they have not been given more chance to operate in the manner in which I believe an advisory council should. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the government has been advising the advisory council, rather than the advisory council advising the government, and to me that seems the wrong way to do things.
I sincerely hope the minister will see to it that this advisory council on rehabilitation will be given a real chance to do useful work in this important field. I believe there is a great need for a rehabilitation program, both physical and occupational, to be operated in co-operation with the provinces. The purpose of it should be to look after the needs of those people in industry who, through disease or accident, are prevented from continuing to earn their own living.
The kind of program I have in mind is the one which was operated with such conspicuous success at the end of the last war, and which dealt so successfully with a great number of disabled veterans. Every effort was made to cure a man's disability, and if that was found to be impossible, then he was taught a trade. This enabled veterans to be fitted into jobs which they could fill and handle, often better than those who have the full use of their faculties. The reason for that is that a great many disabled people are so anxious to show their employer

Supply-Labour
that they can do a good job, despite their disability, that they work harder and apply themselves more than a person who is perfectly normal in every way. I believe if that kind of program is brought into effect by this government a great many more disabled people will be able to continue to earn their own living than is the case today.
The second suggestion I should like to submit to the minister for his consideration concerns the man or woman who has built up an unemployment insurance credit. They should be able to draw on that credit if sickness or accident prevents them from continuing to work. There is no time at which a man or woman needs unemployment insurance benefits quite so much as when sickness or accident prevents them from working. Not only do they have to maintain themselves and their families, but they have hospital and doctors' bills to pay as well. We must also remember that the unemployment insurance credit which a man or woman has built up is his or hers by right, and is not charity. It exists simply because the man or woman and the employer have contributed toward that unemployment insurance credit for the sole purpose of helping to maintain them if, for some reason, they are prevented from working.
The third matter I want to bring to the minister's attention is the desirability and need of paying a pension, equal to the old age pension, to be paid irrespective of age, to all persons whose disability makes it impossible for them to continue to earn their own living. That is simply in keeping with the principle behind the Old Age Security Act, which pays a pension to people over 70 years of age without a means test because it is assumed that people of that age are no longer able to earn their own living.
I believe that men and women in industry who, because of accident or disease, are prevented from continuing to earn their own living, are often more in need of pensions than many persons over 70 years of age. Sick and disabled people have hospital and doctors' bills to pay in addition to maintaining themselves and their families. That puts a considerably greater strain on their finances than is put on the finances of those over 70 who, in many instances-I would say in most instances-are still sound in wind and limb. For that reason I believe the principle behind the old age pension, which is excellent in every way, applies to those disabled people in industry to an even greater degree. For that reason I believe these people should be paid a pension if the doctors of the unemployment insurance commission certify upon examination that they are prevented from continuing to earn their own living. I would appreciate

it if the minister would comment on the suggestions I have made at an appropriate time later in this debate.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: This is an item with reference to the annuities act. The minister knows that we have asked him questions about this a number of times during the session, and some remarks were made on it today by my colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I realize that we face a barrier so far as this session is concerned in the statement made by the Prime Minister a few days ago that no legislation amending the annuities act would be introduced at this session. Nevertheless, that statement by the Prime Minister did not preclude the possibility of an amendment being brought in at the next session, and we urge that that be done. We should like to hear from the Minister of Labour what the situation is and whether there is a reasonable prospect that a bill similar to the one that was not proceeded with last session might be introduced at the next session of parliament.

I shall take only two or three minutes on this item. The government is proposing to spend this year $956,386 on the administration of the annuities act. Incidentally, that is an increase of about $98,000 over a year ago. I want to say at once that I, along with other members of this group, certainly support the annuities act, at least the principle of it, and I concur in most of what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
The original purpose of this act was to encourage people of modest means to make provision for their old age, and I think the act has been at least moderately successful in doing that. I hope the minister will announce, when he brings in amendments to the legislation, that the scope will be extended and the ceilings increased. But there is one feature of the present act I do not like, and I am speaking personally. Out in Saskatchewan we have a government insurance office. That company sells insurance to the people of Saskatchewan at rates considerably below those which prevailed formerly. For the most part they sell insurance at approximately cost. Nevertheless the corporation is expected to pay its way as it goes along. It seems to me that the federal government might take a lesson from the Saskatchewan insurance office in so far as these annuities are concerned. Why should the annuities branch not pay its way as it goes along?

In other words, Mr. Chairman, I believe that federal annuities should be sold at cost, approximately, but not at a loss. If the branch did that, I believe they could still sell annuities considerably cheaper than the insurance companies can sell them. I believe, and believe very strongly, that premium rates charged on these government annuities should first of all cover the cost of administration, and second the solvency of the fund. I can see no reason whatever why the taxpayers of Canada should be called upon to subsidize a scheme which is used by only a minority of the population many of whom are not in need of such subsidy.
May 1 refer the committee for a moment to the details of the estimate. They are contained on page 237. Altogether we are spending $956,000 on administration. The annuity contracts issued last year totalled 21,775, according to page 24 of the minister's report. In other words, last year the administration costs of the annuities which were issued amounted to about $44 each. This bill the taxpayers of Canada had to pay. It does not seem very sensible to me.
We have 189 employees in this department. I hope that the day will come when the volume of these annuities can be increased. At the same time I find it strange that the taxpayers of Canada should be paying the wages of those employees, instead of the people who are benefiting-i.e. the holders of the annuities. Week after week people are saying something should be done to bring down the high cost of government. Surely this is a good place to start to trim the costs. I believe the annuities act, as I said a moment ago, is a most worth-while piece of legislation, and I hope it will be enlarged; I hope it will be expanded. But I do believe annuities should be sold at cost, and should not require annual payments from the taxpayers to keep them going.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about annuities, because I have discussed the matter on other occasions and t would not want this opportunity to pass without stating my views. Then I shall say that a good deal of pressure was put upon the government to have it raised to $200 a month. The only way to reduce those rates is to get out and obtain more business. That may not be popular with the insurance companies; but then they will have to reduce their rates if they want to keep in line.
