The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 10, consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation -Mr. Larson-Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.
On section 1-Incorporation.

Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to speak tonight on this bill, letter O of the Senate, to incorporate Boundary Pipeline Corporation, for the purpose of talking out the bill. Hon. members on the opposition side of the house were complaining that the Liberal members were reluctant to debate this pipe line bill. However, I have no hesitation in letting the house know how I feel toward it.
The first fuel used in Winnipeg, Mr. Chairman, was wood. The cost at that time was mostly the cost of transportation.
Look out for your head.

The same applies now to lignite coal, which is mined in Saskatchewan. The same can be said of the coal we are importing from Alberta. Freight rates have risen to the point where at the present time it is almost impossible or prohibitive to carry on industry and to supply heating facilities. For instance, in cities like Calgary, Edmonton and Medicine Hat the use of cheap natural gas has been a virtual boon to industry. The Boundary Pipeline Corporation should be commended for its proposal to bring natural gas to the people of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, thus enabling the cities I have mentioned to prosper and look forward to a great future.
Many hon. members of the opposition have talked about an all-Canadian route. Last year I supported the all-Canadian route of a pipe line to Vancouver, for which a charter was granted. Work is well under way at the present time, and it is expected to be completed by 1954. As I said, there has been much talk about an all-Canadian route. As indicated in report No. 4 of the minutes of proceedings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, which deals with this bill, it was moved by the

hon. member for Fort William that an amendment be made to section 6 of the bill, which deals with the power to construct and operate a pipe line-
-within the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba or outside Canada construct, purchase, lease or otherwise acquire-
And so on. The hon. member for Fort William moved an amendment:
That paragraph (a) of clause 6 be amended by inserting after the word "lines" in line 23 thereof the words: provided that the main pipe line or lines for the transmission and transportation of gas and oil shall be located entirely within Canada.
Hon. members will see, as it is set out at page 108 of the proceedings of the committee, this amendment was accepted by a vote of 15 to 7. In view of what has been said I should have thought the hon. member for Brandon, who I am sorry is not in his seat this evening, would certainly have made a plea on behalf of the people and the industry of that great city to have the charter of this pipe line bill approved by parliament so the citizens of Brandon, in general, would have the benefit of natural gas.
Then, coming farther east to Winnipeg, I would have expected that that great free enterpriser, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, would have been on his feet working for the city of Winnipeg, that great industrial centre, and would have made his contribution to encourage the building of a natural gas pipe line which would serve the city and his constituents.
What about Portage la Prairie?

Portage la Prairie will speak for itself. Surely a matter of such great importance cannot be overlooked at this time. Those of us in the west who are fortunate enough to have this great natural resource should make an all-out effort to develop it and make cheap natural gas available for industrial purposes and the heating of private homes in Saskatchewan and Manitoba, for the benefit of our constituents.
I ask hon. members to give their sanction and approval now to the passage of this bill, thus enabling the people of Manitoba and Saskatchewan to obtain as soon as possible this cheap means of heating. The citizens of Winnipeg, the citizens of the whole of Manitoba, those of the town of Beausejour, which is the hub of activity in the constituency I have the honour to represent, and also the people in Pine Falls, which is the centre of the Manitoba pulp and paper industry, will certainly welcome this great industrial and heating fuel. Natural gas will improve and develop the industry now located in Pine
Boundary Pipeline Corporation Falls. The export of paper from this company to the United States represents almost a third of Manitoba's total budget.
Whoever wrote that speech is a clever fellow.

And you are looking at him, right now. As the source of supply gets greater, certainly there will be a possibility in the future of extending the gas pipe line to Ontario and Quebec. But surely, for the good of Canada, we cannot afford at this time to hold back industry in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Any attempt to conduct a filibuster on this bill would have the effect of creating a monopoly for other pipe line companies which have already been granted charters, and would thereby prevent the company now making application from competing. It would have the effect of eliminating from the field what might very well be a most competent company and one highly capable of carrying on this great enterprise, which would result in placing natural gas at the disposal of the people of Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
The board of transport commissioners and the Alberta conservation board will have the opportunity to look thoroughly into the economic aspects of this pipe line. Our action now in passing the bill would give the company an equal opportunity to place the facts before the board of transport commissioners so that body might look into all aspects of the matter and the details of the company's organization.

I asked him how many cubic feet of gas the proposed pipe line would carry. His answer, as reported at page 3098 of Hansard, was as follows:

I would say just about as many as
the hairs on the hon. gentleman's head. If we could count the hairs on his head, we could pretty nearly tell how many.

If we were tc follow the suggestion of the hon. member foi

I shall now answer the question I asked the hon. member just to show what he knew about the pipe line. Evidently he did not know anything about them. It is estimated the natural gas carried by this pipe line in the first year will be 42,400,000 cubic feet per day. Again I ask my hon. friends opposite, and especially the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Fraser Valley, to give the people of Manitoba and Saskatchewan an opportunity to use this important commodity of natural gas which will make industry in the west prosper for future generations. We helped you, so we ask you to help us and in doing so I am sure that by working together we can make this a better Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I am certain you will agree that the eloquent plea of the hon. member for Springfield should not go unanswered. permit them to be served along with Manitoba and Saskatchewan, then I would hope he would vote against this bill. I would hope he would agree with us and oppose the granting of this charter and support a proposition under which it is intended to serve the whole of Canada.

I do not think it is relevant to the bill. The hon. member made a passing reference to that, and I think more than passing references have been made by various speakers who have taken part in the debate. It was at that point I intervened and asked the hon. member to direct his remarks to the bill.

In discussing this bill an hon. member is surely entitled to deal with the policy which was explained to the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines by the representatives of this group of men who are applying for a charter. That is all the hon. member has been doing.

speechtext: That is a different proposition. The hon. member may have his own opinion, but it just so happens that the chairman has a different one. In any event the fact is that I called the hon. member for Kamloops to order, that point has now been decided, and he has the floor.

Mr. Chairman, I think I grasp the point of order you have raised, and I shall

say no more about it except to say that I may have used the words "government policy" and if so I assent to your correction. The purpose of my remarks was to indicate the basis upon which I oppose the bill and why, therefore, I consider that the gentlemen applying for incorporation under the clause we are discussing should not be granted that incorporation. That was the purpose of the remarks I was making, and I take it from what Your Honour has said that, provided I do not get into the wide field of controversy as to the different views on the general subject of the exploitation of our resources, I am nevertheless in order in saying, with respect to the way it is proposed that this particular pipe line shall go, why I feel these gentlemen should not have their incorporation.
That is what I shall endeavour to do for the remainder of the time which I had intended to speak this evening. It is because this company, according to the evidence its sponsors gave before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, intends to export the gas which they would carry to Winnipeg south to the United States instead of carrying it eastward in order to serve the eastern provinces that I am opposed to its incorporation. In that connection the considerations before the committee are very much the same as those which were before the committee on earlier occasions when pipe-line incorporations were being debated. I wish to point out and emphasize at this stage that the reasons which induced me and others on this side of the house, the hon. member for Fraser Valley and anyone else who may be opposed to the bill, to oppose it are not simply because the company intends to export what may be a surplus of gas, although I think I should observe that the question of whether there will be a surplus is by no means settled. It is not simply because they intend to export what they might claim to be a surplus of gas that we oppose them. It is because they intend to export it to the United States in such a way as to deny the use of that gas in perpetuity to the people of eastern Canada who have shown very clearly that they want and need the gas.
It is on the basis of the principle, therefore, that Canada's resources should be used for the benefit of Canada first that we stand squarely opposed to the incorporation of this company. It is the same policy exactly as that in connection with our opposition to the incorporation of companies in earlier years which had expressed their desire to export gas to the United States to the prejudice of Canada. What we say is that there should be

no denial of the export of surplus gas after Canada's needs have been met, but that we should rather follow an active policy of development of the Canadian economy by using Canada's gas and other resources so as to give employment and opportunity to Canadians.
There is a very interesting development, Mr. Chairman, which has taken place in connection with this whole gas pipe-line controversy as is shown by the discussion now going on before the board of transport commissioners. It has already been pointed out to Your Honour and to the committee that the gentlemen who are seeking to be incorporated here are connected with, and the company will be a subsidiary of, the Fish Engineering Corporation of the United States. Your Honour will remember that two years ago we incorporated another natural gas pipe-line company, namely Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. That company is now before the board of transport commissioners here in Ottawa seeking a permit to carry natural gas through this line from the northern Alberta and Peace river area, through northern British Columbia, down through the centre of our province to Vancouver and on to Seattle and Portland.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that one of the companies which had also sought incorporation for the same purpose-that is, to carry gas west-a company called Prairie Transmission Lines Limited, was a subsidiary in the same way of the Fish Engineering Corporation. It is further interesting to note that the Fish Engineering Corporation, having failed to get this company incorporated to carry that gas, is now before the board of transport commissioners in Ottawa opposing the application of the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. I point that fact out to hon. members-and particularly to the hon. member for Springfield-who have urged that we do not take what they call a small view with regard to denying the export of natural gas to the United States. I point out to them that this company, having failed in its own application to get a company incorporated earlier for the transportation of gas in western Canada, is now before the board of transport commissioners seeking by every means within its power to prevent the Westcoast company from getting on with that job which would be to the tremendous benefit of our province.
For the benefit of the committee I think I should read a report on this matter appearing in the Vancouver Sun of Wednesday, June 11. It is headed "From the Vancouver Sim Ottawa Bureau" and reads:
A sharp word battle developed before the board of transport commissioners today as a U.S. firm
Boundary Pipeline Corporation tried to block Vancouver's chances of getting natural gas from Alberta and B.C.'s Peace river.
The debate occurred during hearing of the Canadian-owned Westcoast Transmission Company's application to build a 700-mile gas pipe line to Vancouver from northwest Alberta through central B.C.
Opposing the application is the Pacific Northwest Pipeline Company which wants to pipe gas from Texas to American cities in the Pacific northwest.
That is the Pacific Northwest Pipeline Company which is the subsidiary of the Fish Engineering Corporation. The article continues:
This company would not service B.C.'s lower mainland.
Westcoast Transmission has offered to continue its pipe line south to Seattle, Portland and other U.S. centres. It was admitted the American market must be secured if the pipe line is to be built at all.
Several sharp exchanges between D. P. McDonald, Q.C., of Calgary, appearing for Westcoast, and S. Bruce Smith, Q.C., of Edmonton, spokesman for Northwest, featured the morning session.
I do not want to read the whole of this article, Mr. Chairman, but perhaps it is better to put it in the words of the article here because the tone will appear more clearly:
When A. Bruce Robertson, B.C. Electric vicepresident, testified that the BCE was willing to distribute natural gas in Vancouver, New Westminster and Victoria areas for Westcoast, Smith jumped to his feet.
"Does Westcoast have contracts with gas distributing utilities in Seattle, Portland, Tacoma and other cities in that region?" he wanted to know.
McDonald interjected that letters of contract from the American utilities would be submitted to the board, to the obvious surprise of the Northwest representative.
Then acid words were exchanged as McDonald hammered at the fact that Prairie Transmission Limited, nominally represented by Smith at the hearing, was "100 per cent owned by Pacific Northwest Pipelines."
Dr. Charles R. Hetherington of New York, natural gas expert for the pipe line firm of Ford, Bacon and Davis, said that if the Northwest company blocked Westcoast from the Washington-Oregon markets, "Vancouver would be without (natural) gas."
When Smith snorted audibly, Hetherington repeated his statement, adding: "Canada would be without the benefits of the explorations of natural gas in the Peace river sections of Alberta and British Columbia."
The point of this, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me is clear. Here is a case where a Canadian company, Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, which proposes to serve Canada first, is admittedly dependent for the whole success of its enterprise on getting into the United States market of the northwest states. As soon as its own company was defeated in an effort to pipe natural gas to the United States, this Fish Engineering Corporation announced it was going to bring gas into the northwest states from Texas and thus block the efforts of the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. That is what we can see now. This is the attempt we see being made

Boundary Pipeline Corporation before the board of transport commissioners in accordance with the report which I have just read. It seems to me-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. May I ask the hon. member whether the application of the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited has been decided upon by the board of transport commissioners?
Not yet.

speechtext: Therefore the matter is sub judice and the hon. member should not deal with it. May I say I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to get into a controversy with you as to the meaning of the doctrine of sub judice. I am not discussing the merits of the application of Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, as they are being argued before the board.
I am simply drawing to Your Honour's attention the arguments which are being put up before the board by somebody opposing that application, namely a company which is a subsidiary of the same company which is now applying for incorporation of this company in Canada. I am pointing out to Your Honour-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon, member will agree that the line is rather hard to draw. If he were the presiding officer, and if reference was made to a matter that was before a court or a board such as the board of transport commissioners, I think he would point out that it has been the rule in this chamber that hon. members may not refer to such matters.

I think Your Honour will agree that it is permissible to point out, without comment, that the application of this Canadian company is being opposed by a company which is a subsidiary of the Fish Engineering Corporation, the same company which now asks through another subsidiary for incorporation of this Boundary Pipeline Corporation before the committee. I think Your Honour would agree that it is permissible to point out that fact. I hope Your Honour will agree-and I will go carefully so Your Honour can stop me if you think I am overstepping the mark-that it is permissible to point out that the company opposing Westcoast, which is the same in effect as the company now trying to get this application through, is seeking to do that by denying to Westcoast the United States market in the Pacific northwest without which Westcoast's enterprise or operation would be uneconomical. I just want to point out and stress this fact and leave the matter there, because I think it is that fact that Canadians should bear


in mind when they have before them an application, as we have here in this committee, by that very same subsidiary of that same Fish Engineering Corporation, to incorporate this Boundary Pipeline Corporation which would again export gas to the United States and would have the effect of permanently denying Alberta gas to Ontario and Quebec.
I have already dealt with the fact that the reason we are opposed to this application is not that we are opposed to giving gas to the prairies, particularly to Saskatchewan and Manitoba but, as is indicated clearly from the discussion, that there will be only one pipe line carrying gas eastward, and if that pipe line goes down into the United States from Winnipeg it means that gas will never reach the eastern provinces of Canada.
In this connection I think it is interesting to recall that the argument taking place here is the old argument which took place in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway, except it is that argument in reverse. Hon. members will recall that in those days, when the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway was being mooted, it was suggested that the railway should not be built north of the great lakes but that instead United States railways south of the great lakes should be used for moving goods and passengers from Canada's eastern seaboard to the western portion of our country, and that only west of the great lakes should the line go north and be built in Canada. Today we have a case where history is reversing itself. In those days it was the east which was going to build the west. Here we have a case in connection with gas where the west is able to make a contribution to the east, and the east is looking with anxious eyes to the bringing of this resource down here from the west. It is the reverse of the old position.
We find some people in this house, however, still supporting the old argument that Canada's resources should be sent down into the United States. We, on the contrary, say that the line, just as was said in connection with the railway, must be built north of the great lakes through Canada first so as to serve Canada. Then if there is any surplus left by all means let us export it south of the border. It is interesting to recall that the same principles which applied in connection with the railway debate, and which I submit were valid at that time, are equally valid at this time-indeed, have more application-and that we from the west should be just as insistent that the resources of Canada now in the west should be brought down to serve the east, just as most patriotic Canadians were that the railway coming from

the east to the west should be built through Canada first. We in western Canada, and British Columbia particularly, have good reason to oppose the incorporation of this line which will work to the detriment to our friends in Ontario and Quebec, because those who recall past debates-the member for Fraser Valley, the member for Vancouver-Quadra and those of my friends in the C.C.F. party to my left-will recall that we had a full measure of wholehearted co-operation from the members from Ontario and Quebec last year in our effort to secure the movement of gas and oil to western Canada through the incorporation of companies which would serve Canada first instead of sending it to the United States to the detriment of our province.
I recall that we had support from the hon. member for Labelle, the hon. member for Three Rivers, the hon. member for Huron North, the hon. member for Greenwood, the hon. member for Broadview, the hon. member for Victoria, the senior member for Queens, the hon. member for York South, the hon. member for St. John's West, the hon. member for Royal, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough; the leader of this party, the hon. member for Carleton; the hon. member for St. John's East, as well as many others. I do not think we would be showing any sense of gratitude if now, when they are so vitally interested in getting western gas into Ontario and Quebec, we were not to support their position but were to allow the incorporation of this company which will ship the natural resource down into the United States so it can never be obtained in eastern Canada.
I am impressed, Mr. Chairman, with something that no member can overlook in connection with this debate, a fact which admittedly has been referred to on several previous occasions but which it does not hurt to remind ourselves of again, namely that the responsible authorities in Ontario and Quebec have made it clear that they are very anxious now to have that gas. They feel that the only way they can be assured of a supply of gas is to have Alberta gas piped down here. I pointed out earlier in my remarks the tactics pursued by this United States company when their own interests are at stake, and the way they are opposing the application of the Westcoast Transmission Company to serve the British Columbia area. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, if they will resort to those methods in this case there is no reason for us to suppose that United States companies would make any
Boundary Pipeline Corporation deal which would guarantee to Ontario and Quebec a supply of gas from the United States.
If the supply of gas from Alberta to Ontario and Quebec is denied, then the only place they can look is to the United States. It is obvious from what has happened in the United States federal power commission, as well as the tactics of some of these United States companies, that Ontario and Quebec would not be on safe ground in relying on an agreement being reached to obtain a supply of gas from the United States. We find the Ontario minister of mines saying, as reported in the press of January 22:
. . . our policy is going to be to encourage a trans-Canada pipe line both as a source of fuel for Ontario and Quebec and as a national defence safeguard.
And then he went on to say:
We see no other answer than an all-Canadian pipe line.
Then I submit that hon. members in this house should, without question, reject an application for incorporation such as we have before us today which would deny Ontario the supply of gas which is so vital.
I do not want to forget, either, that the premier of Quebec, who after all in this connection is the spokesman for the province, has said much the same thing with regard to the interest of his province in obtaining a supply of gas from western Canada. This is what the premier of Quebec said on March 29, according to the Montreal Star:
Quebec was in favour of importing natural gas from Alberta rather than from Texas, he said, to support Canadian industry . . .
The premier said nothing had yet been decided as to whether pipe lines would be built or not into Quebec province. But he said, if natural gas is to be imported it will not be United States gas.
The premier said Quebec preferred to import gas from Alberta because it was preferable to support a Canadian industry, not subject "to a foreign authority."
So as I say, when we from the west-

Supply-Labour SUPPLY

197. Training payments to the provinces, $4,027,000.
On this item, Mr. Chairman, has the minister the amount that was allotted for Newfoundland, and how much was spent?
The allotment last year for Newfoundland was $65,800, and the total payments out of that allotment were $49,227.

I want to point to the situation in British Columbia where the provincial government, with all compliments to the minister, in co-operation with the federal government have established a vocational training institute in the city of Vancouver. I do not intend to say anything about that institute because it is doing a tremendous job; but I do point out that all the province of British Columbia is not situated within the confines of the city of Vancouver. We in Burnaby, a community of 60,000 people, consider that we should have some vocational training facilities of our own.
In 1951 the number of pupils enrolled in the institute in Vancouver was 5,517. Because of the good work of the department some 500 of those pupils were placed in jobs after the completion of their courses. But the situation there is very serious. I know of a number of young people from my riding who have not been able to get into that vocational institute. As other hon. members from British Columbia will most likely tell you, we feel that our young people are entitled to the same advantages that are obtained by the young people in the city of Vancouver.
With all due respect to the minister, I believe that the department is going at this in the wrong way. I believe the institute is a very fine operation, and I support it wholeheartedly. But that institute takes the position that young men and women must have left high school before they can take part in these courses. As I have said on other occasions in the house, I believe we are going at this matter wrongly. There are young men and women in our high schools who, because of the financial difficulties of their parents, will never be able to go to university. In my own riding in 1951 only 20 per cent of our senior high school students could afford to go to university. That left 80 per cent of our senior high school pupils at loose ends. For instance, they cannot attend the vocational institute of Vancouver because there is no 
room for them. What happens? Perhaps 50 per cent of these young men and women go out to jobs for which they are not fitted, or perhaps they do not want them; but they are forced, through financial circumstances of the family, to go to work for which they are not fitted and to which they do not want to go in the first place.
There is money to be spent in vocational training, and I think in the years to come, perhaps not this year, the minister could consider what I have suggested in this house before with respect to vocational training, and start in a general way on the high school level. Our young men and women should be given the opportunity before they leave high school, or a least have it suggested to them through practical application, that there are jobs in this world available to them, if we can give them some help, rather than going out and accepting a job for which they are not fitted and perhaps to which they do not wish to go.
I know of some five young men in one school in my riding. I spoke to them during the time I was home quite lately. They told me that they have to go to work in the woods. They were not fitted for it; they wanted to go to university, but their fathers could not afford it. So they were going into the woods when school was over. That is not fair. Canada is far too big a country to allow our young men and women to take work for which they are not fitted and do not want. I am quite sure that if I place my position before the minister he will understand it and will consider doing a little more for general vocational training in our senior high schools.
I repeat what I said when I first rose to speak. The young men and women in my riding cannot get to the vocational institute in Vancouver because there is no room for them. Instructors are available, but there are no classrooms for these young men and women. The average course in that institute takes six or seven months. There are some people in that institute who will be there for two years. Vacancies are not occurring fast enough. I would suggest to the minister that some of this money spent on vocational training, instead of going into that institute and other institutes across Canada, could be spent in this way. We should consider this high school problem.
While I am on my feet, if the chairman will allow me, I should like to refer to item 198. I have a few words to say on it. In his estimates the minister calls for a decrease of $116,000 in this item. I doubt very much whether that meets with the minister's approval. I wonder how much the treasury

board had to do with this decrease. I am not going to be able to put over my idea of vocational training for high school pupils if the minister is going to be forced to reduce his estimates for capital construction.
So far as the $1 million odd is concerned- the minister will correct me if I am wrong- the province of British Columbia is allocated 6 per cent of the total. That amounts to $62,000 or $63,000 this year. I do not think you can build two classrooms at present construction costs for $62,000 or $63,000, regardless of the equipment it takes. I happen to know from my school board work before I came here that an ordinary classroom will cost you $25,000 to build and equip today. Therefore what does the minister expect to give to British Columbia with $63,000? What does the minister expect to get by way of capital construction for vocational training for that amount? I may have the idea wrong but the inspector of schools in Burnaby has told me by letter, which I hold in my hand, that we are entitled to 6 per cent of the total.
I do not think that is sufficient. I think the minister should be getting $10 million instead of $1 million for capital construction of vocational training institutes across Canada. And if my words can be of any assistance to the minister in his negotiations with the treasury board, then he can take them, because he has my full co-operation.

I have the report for 1951. On page 78, table 1 deals with youth training, and we have the allotment for Newfoundland of $20,000, of which the sum of $6,000 was spent. Thirty-eight university students took youth training. I wonder whether the minister has the comparable figures for 1951-52. Can he give me a general idea as to who is entitled to apply for this?
The allotment for 1951-52 was $15,000, and the total payments $11,605.
Has the minister the number of students? Is this on the same basis as the previous year? Does this grant apply to university undergraduates?
Yes.
Does the minister know how many?
I have not the number of students involved here.
Is any student entitled to apply for this grant?

The whole selection-and this applies also to the suggestions made in the early part of the remarks of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-of students, who
Supply-Labour
shall qualify as to ages, and whether they shall be based on need and so on, is made by the provincial authorities. Provided the work is carried out in a general way in accord with the principles set out, our task is to mainly assist in the work the provincial authorities are doing by making grants in aid. I think it is true that, in the main, the boys and girls in Newfoundland who qualify for these courses are those who have reached certain educational standards, and who have some need for assistance in this kind of training.
I should like to find out on what basis the allocation of money to the provinces for capital expenditure is made.

In a general way it is based upon the population between certain age groups. I believe it is from 16 to 19. I will admit that in the very interesting and continuous discussions and negotiations with the provinces, if for instance one province cannot or will not use all its allotment, then we do try to make the best use of the money available. Consequently it may not always work out exactly in the same ratio to that of the youthful population I mentioned.

Then can it be said that if an allotment is made to a province on the basis of the number of young people within that age group, and that province does not use the money, another province which is more ready to make use of an extra amount can apply for and receive a further allotment?
In some cases. We do not encourage it, though, because we like every province to feel that they are having an opportunity to utilize their allotments up to the end of the fiscal year.

What I am driving at, ultimately, is this. I believe the point made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond was well taken. It may be that the minister has not enough money in this vote, and that he could use more. The point is how to get it. I am wondering if the minister could say he could use more money, if the provinces are ready to use it properly, under the policy laid down by the department. Would he say, for instance, that the $1,134,000 provided in item 198 is all the provinces are ready to use at this time under the department's policy, or would it be possible for him to spend considerably more money under that same policy and with the co-operation of the provinces?

That is a fair question. The direct answer is that we could usefully spend more money than this. I was glad to have the representations this afternoon because, when the supplementary estimates are presented, I would hope that the suggestions

Supply-Labour
tonight for an additional amount in this respect might support my request for more at that time.
You have our backing.

I take it the minister is not very familiar with the details of the operation of the vocational school in Newfoundland, because it seems to me that in no case was the allotment spent. 200. To provide for expenditures incurred in implementing recommendations of the national advisory council on manpower, and for the administrative costs of the council, $107,950.

I promised the hon. member for Hamilton West, who could not be here this evening, and the hon. members for Cape Breton South and Broadview that I would make some comment on the national advisory council on manpower. In the opinion of some hon. members this advisory council has not fulfilled the high expectations they had for
Supply-Labour
it when I announced the setting up of the council in the house a year ago last spring.
The personnel making up this advisory council I think is well known to all members; if not, the names are on the record. It will be recalled that it was appointed at a period when there was a great wave of concern throughout the North American continent with regard to the emergency which was then beginning and which has continued down to the present time.
The intention was not, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested, to make this an administrative or directing or day to day working body, but rather to have available as supplementary to this House of Commons the advice of a group of people who were distinguished representatives of various fields of endeavour. Organized labour and1 organized management were well represented. The hon. member for Cape Breton South suggested that men from the shops should sit on the committee. If organized labour felt that was a better representation I am sure they would have said so. As it turned out they nominated national leaders to represent them on this body.
This council has held meetings, and the hon. member for Broadview has suggested that the results of those meetings must be judged by the reports. That is true to a degree. The reports in the press are based upon news releases. For reasons which the council felt were adequate the press was not present at the meetings of the council.
I can assure the committee that there has been no effort on the part of the Minister of Labour or any member of the government to dictate or even suggest to this body what they should recommend to the government. I felt it was my duty to invite the right hon. Minister of Defence Production, whose need for manpower was then and is now very great, to come before this council and tell them' what his plans were and to receive criticism and suggestions.
It was in the same vein that I invited the Minister of National Defence to attend. Since immigration into the country affects our man and womanpower resources the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was similarly invited to attend. Although I have not yet had an opportunity to do so, it is my intention to ask the Minister of Agriculture to appear before the council. I now invite the hon. member for Broadview to sit in at the next meeting.

That will be an improvement.

Supply-Labour

I am sure it will. While nothing spectacular has resulted from the meetings of this council, as far as I am concerned I have been quite happy about the work it has accomplished. For one thing, from the very beginning of the emergency following Korea it has provided a ready outlet for the expression of opinions on the part of organized labour and organized management sitting around the same table.
It has been asked why we have so many high government officials sitting in under the chairmanship of my deputy minister and the secretary of the privy council. The reason the deputy ministers or senior officers of the departments of labour, defence, immigration and defence production were asked to be a part of the committee was so the advisers of the government might be in originally on the suggestions made by organized labour, industry, veterans, women, farmers and so on represented on the council.
I should like to express my gratitude to those who have served on the council, and I can assure the committee that we do not consider it as a body to pass on what the department has done. We have asked it to criticize or make suggestions on what has been done. The apprenticeship conference called this spring was a direct result of suggestions that were made. The work that has been going on with respect to the needs related to our whole manpower picture in the larger emergency is a direct result of suggestions that have been made. Seasonal employment, which has been discussed here, the placement of older men and women and the project which is so close to the heart of the hon. member for Broadview, rehabilitation of the physically disabled, have all been discussed. I will mention typical subjects that have been under discussion, and I am sure the council has provided guidance not only to my officials but to those of other government departments. Subjects that have been discussed are immigration, the present manpower situation, seasonal unemployment, technical and scientific personnel, supply and demand in the professions, placement of older workers, farm labour, vocational training, rehabilitation of the physically handicapped, and preparation for any phase of manpower development as the result of a worsening of the emergency with which we are faced at the present time.

Would the minister give us some explanation of the details of this item as given on page 244? I notice, for instance, that in the estimates there is an amount of nearly $85,000 for stationery and office equipment and it appears that there are no employees there to use it. There are

no estimates for the payment of employees other than $12,000 for allowances and expenses of board members. Last year there was $20,000 for stationery and office equipment and this year the estimates call for $84,000. That is well over $100,000 for equipment for this office in two years. What sort of staff is there in the office?

My hon. friend is quite right. The personnel are not there to use the equipment but the answer is related to the last item in my reply a moment ago. As my hon. friend will recall, two years ago when my estimates were before the committee I was very strongly advised that we, in conjunction with other departments, should go a long way to anticipate the amount of paper work that might be involved within our departments in the event of a worsening of the national emergency. Consequently, to have the paper work on a large manpower program carried out involves the preparation of forms and the obtaining of the type of material and equipment required. That is why this item is there.
Who is to make use of all this paper? There is no staff listed here.
We have not reached yet, thank heaven, a full-out emergency.

I thank the minister for his explanatory remarks about the operations of the advisory council. I think potentially it is a very useful body, and I believe members of parliament would obtain a great deal of most useful information if they could be advised of the opinions expressed by members of the council on matters that are of tremendous importance to all of us. When news releases are made by the department I would suggest that the opinions of the members of the advisory council should be recorded, as well as the reports of government departments that are given to members of the advisory council. I would also suggest that when such news releases are issued, they should be made available to all members of parliament as well as to members of the press, which is the present practice. 1 think we would get a great deal of information from these news releases.
The specific purpose of this item is to provide for expenditures incurred in implementing recommendations of the national advisory council on manpower, and for the administrative costs of the council. Could the minister advise us what recommendations have been made during the past year and a half by the council, and which of those recommendations have been implemented by the government?

That would be quite a long story. May I refer to my hon. friend's first

suggestion. I shall be very happy to comply with it, and if it appears to be the desire I am prepared to go even farther and send out to members a more detailed analysis. I would hate to go through the record in a hurried fashion and reply to what he has asked with respect to the several meetings that have been held, but I will make a very compact abstract of those meetings and make it available for members of the house who may require it. I will be glad to send one to my hon. friend.

I want to thank the minister very much for his willingness and co-operation, and also for his kind offer to allow me to attend the next meeting of the manpower council. In passing I should like to suggest that the same procedure could be adopted with regard to the newly formed advisory council on rehabilitation. I think members of the house would be just as interested in the proceedings of that advisory council as they are in the manpower council, and if the same sensible suggestion the minister has made about advising us as to what goes on at the meetings of the manpower council could be carried out with respect to this new council I think it would be a good thing.

That, Mr. Chairman, is an outline of the order in council. As to some of the important questions that I know are in the mind of the hon. member for Broadview and perhaps in the minds of other hon. members, I should like them to be allowed to stand until the executive of this committee has had an opportunity to prove itself. Mr. Ian Campbell has taken on his new duties as from the first of this month. He is this week end attending
IMr. Gregg.]
the large social welfare councils that are being held in the city of Quebec. He has provided on the special council a panel which is dealing with the rehabilitation of the physically handicapped. When that meeting is over he is going to start at Newfoundland, I believe, and visit each provincial capital, calling upon the representative in that capital who is on the national council and upon those who are so capably engaged, in voluntary agencies, in this work. He will thus be working from the ground up rather than from the top down.
The members of the council are all technical people in this field. They all know what it is about. I think I interpret then-general view when I say they all feel that this problem is one that should be approached on a national basis-whatever each province might do, as has been done now in Ontario- through the voluntary agencies, provincial governments and federal departments concerned, and that the stress should be on the medical and occupational refitting of the person for work so that he will be able to earn his own living. Out of that, of course, will come some who will not be able to work at all, but if our veterans' experience holds reasonably well there will be few in that category.

I thank the minister very much for his remarks explaining the function of this new body. Mr. Chairman, with respect to unemployment insurance, we are having a debate on that subject on a bill which the minister has before the house. At this point, however, I should like to ask the minister what progress he is making in a city like Winnipeg, and perhaps in other cities, in getting better accommodation for the unemployment insurance commission and the national employment service which is associated with that commission. I should like to point out in the first place that there are a number of offices of the unemployment insurance commission in Winnipeg, and for the most part they are on streets that are off the main thoroughfares, and in the main they are in rather old buildings. The minister's colleague the Minister of National Revenue seems to fare much better. The place where the taxes are collected is a fine building. I do not know what the idea is, whether they want to make you feel it is a nice place to go.
Honey for the flies.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Yes; and where you get stuck, too. This function which is performed by the unemployment insurance commission is rather important. The number of people that come and go in those offices, both in connection with unemployment insurance and in connection with employment placement,

Supply-Labour
must be very large indeed. It would seem to me that an effort should be made to get a reasonably choice location, and also to get all the unemployment insurance offices under one roof. Naturally, an effort should be made to locate it in some place which is not only choice in the sense of being attractive, but choice in the sense of being readily accessible to the large number of people who would have to go there.
I believe the matter has been under consideration; I would hope it has, because of the scattered nature of the set-up in Winnipeg. Can the minister say what progress has been made? I can assure my hon. friend that we are very much concerned that the offices shall be-

speechtext: Just as good as the income tax offices.

speechtext: I take it from what the minister has said that the Winnipeg situation is specifically under consideration. Does the minister agree with me that it would be desirable to have all the unemployment insurance offices located under one roof in a more desirable location than is now the case?

Well, I would make one reservation there, of course. There is a great advantage in having offices dispersed for the convenience of the workers who may live in outlying sections of a large city like Winnipeg. I do not think-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The dispersal at Winnipeg does not meet that qualification. The offices are on William avenue, McDermot avenue and Bannatyne avenue. They are at those different places because you do not have one place in the downtown area that is satisfactory.

whether we should have the offices uptown, or in the central part of the city, or downtown, but we shall take into consideration my hon. friend's remarks.

Has the minister or his department given any consideration to the possibility of reducing the administrative costs of unemployment insurance, or changing the basis under which unemployment insurance is paid so that less bookkeeping and fewer bookkeepers will be required for the administration of the act?

The commission is not an old body. As my hon. friend knows, it was ten years old last year. By the very nature of things it is a very complicated structure, but I can assure him that it is given constant study for improvement. The administrative costs are high. On the other hand, from my observation I am confident that our 200-odd offices across the country dealing with this problem are not overstaffed from the' point of view of the employment service, the service they have to give the public.
As to the wing which deals with the insurance and all the related records, statistics and cards and all the things that I am sure are as mystifying to my hon, friend as they are to me, we have them under study and are making any improvements we can to cut down not only on the cost but also on the amount of paper work involved to do the job.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make an observation on this, again in regard to the question of insurance for fishermen. The sum of $57 million is involved in these two items as the government's contribution toward unemployment insurance, and fishermen get no insurance. In the Daily News, published in St. John's, of April 10, 1952, an editorial appeared which dealt with the statement by the minister. I do not remember the statement but it referred to the difficulties cited by the minister as follows:
The obvious difficulties cited by Labour Minister Gregg as obstacles to the extension of unemployment insurance benefits to Newfoundland fishermen reveal a problem only to be solved by a change in fishing organization or in unemployment insurance procedure.

The editorial goes on to cite what is obvious, that the fisherman sees people getting insurance benefits and he gets nothing. Then they say that not much can be done about it because he is a sort of small capitalist; he is a self-employed person. The article goes on:
The unfortunate aspect of this situation is that many men are turning away from the fisheries to enter insurable employment. And that process can continue to the point where the fishing population of Newfoundland will be sadly and even calamitously diminished in size. That would not be so grave a prospect if alternative employment on a permanent basis were to be readily available but thousands of new jobs cannot be created overnight. Thus abandonment of the fisheries on a large scale could mean excessive competition for other jobs, demands for relief, or substantial migration to the mainland.
The newspaper editor considers that perhaps the best way to deal with it would be reorganization of the fisheries to convert owners and sharemen into wage earners. I cannot say I quite agree with that solution. 1 think it is better for men to have their own business. Then he says:
But the dispersal of the fishing population in a thousand coves and harbours sets up an immediate obstacle to the swift development of a plan of this kind. The only possible alternative would be the evolution of a practicable means of underwriting the security of the producer by assuring him of an adequate reward for his labours. That seems to involve an elastic use of the price support law to cover this specific problem.
It seems to me there is no doubt about it; on the Pacific coast as well as on the Atlantic coast, in Newfoundland and in the maritime provinces, the fishermen are faced with that situation. Some new device must be invented by the minister, or perhaps the Minister of Labour in collaboration with his colleague the Minister of Fisheries. There seems to be a sort of injustice. While I appreciate all that the deputy minister of fisheries has recommended be done for the fishermen, nevertheless that uncertain prospect of poor prices for his fish or a poor catch has the same effect upon his economic fortunes as unemployment has on workers in the factories, and leaves him in a position where he feels he is being treated unjustly. I hope the minister will give consideration to these points I have brought out.

I will promise to comply;
nevertheless I must admit, as my hon. friend outlined at the beginning, that the difficulties are very great. There is the difficulty of the small capitalist who has his own boat and runs his own show, often with one helper, and how to make collections in those cases. Then there is the small farmer in our eastern country who has a farm helper part of the year and is a cutter of pulp wood and pit props the rest of the year. These are questions

that so far we have not found answers to, but we will be glad to keep them ever to the fore.

207.	To provide for the transfer of labour to and from places where employment is available in agriculture and industry and expenses incidental thereto, in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $200,000.

Will the minister explain the difference between this item and item 194? It seems to me there is quite a similarity in the relationship of these two items. I am not objecting to the amount of money spent under this item because I feel it is very important, particularly as far as agriculture in eastern Canada is concerned. I should like the minister to explain the reason for these two items which to me are remarkably similar.

It just happens that that question was anticipated. The unemployment insurance commission vote shown here is to provide for the payment of transportation for federal-sponsored movement of workers to areas of short supply not only for agriculture but also for other industries when the movements are interprovincial in nature. If movements sponsored by the federal government relate to the agricultural worker, 50 per cent of the cost thereof is billed by the unemployment insurance commission to the province, apportioned to the numbers and estimated length of time they are employed in each province, and the amount is charged against the allotment under the farm-labour agreement. Transportation costs shared by the federal government under the farm-labour agreements relate principally to movements within the provincial boundary which are sponsored, with the concurrence of the federal government, by the province and administered by provincial transportation warrants.
