Many of these are small and of only local application. Many can be handled by discussions with the minister, his deputy or some other departmental official. There are only four the discussion of which I propose to inflict upon the committee at this time. I believe all four are of such a nature as to be handled satisfactorily under item 141, and by so doing the committee will be saved watching me bob up and down as each item is called.
The first matter I would draw to the attention of the minister is certainly one related to departmental administration, in that we can get help only if those who administer the department will take action. At first blush it may appear that the matter does not apply at all to the Department of Fisheries, because remedial action would have to be taken by another department of government. However, I think when the Minister of Fisheries is before the committee I am fully justified in asking him, on behalf of the fishing industry, to take an interest in this matter.
I was not in the House of Commons prior to 1949, but it is my understanding that it was the purpose of parliament to exempt from sales tax and excise tax all those articles which go into the earning of a living by either fishermen or farmers. This year we had some amendments to the sales tax extending those exemptions to items used by fishermen which apparently had not been covered before. The exemptions are varied. In general terms I believe they might be said to appear to include everything in the nature of fishing gear, including small ropes, sinkers, floats and the like.
Quite recently it has been found, however, that certain types of fishing plugs and lures, including plastic plugs and certain lures used extensively by commercial fishermen,

were not included and are not at the present time exempted from sales tax. Yet they are just as much a part of the equipment of a commercial fisherman as are nets or other fishing gear.
I am not asking the Minister of Fisheries at the moment to give me a reply in this connection, because I realize he would not be able to do so until the matter had been discussed with the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Revenue and others; but I would ask him, as Minister of Fisheries, to look into the matter. If it is found that the acts as at present worded are such that lures and plugs used by commercial fishermen are now subject to sales tax when sold to commercial fishermen, I would ask him to take the initiative in bringing about an amendment so that what I have no doubt was the original intention of parliament will be carried out, namely that the tools of the trade used by fishermen may be exempt.
The next matter I would refer to the minister and the department is of major concern to a large section of only the Pacific coast. In July of last year we suffered a major calamity out there in the nature of a rockslide. I believe hon. members would have a better picture if it were described as a landslide. It completely blocked the Babine river. That is the river up which pass the vast majority of the sockeye salmon of the whole Skeena river run. Other types of salmon also go up the Babine river to the spawning grounds.
I suggest it is fairly obvious that if salmon do not reach the spawning beds, then four years later there will be a complete failure in the salmon run. The damage done by the Babine river slide was such that last year there was not a very good escapement of sockeye or other salmon to Babine lake. The situation this year may be somewhat the same. If it is not possible, and I think perhaps it is not, to construct in that isolated area a permanent solution to the major calamity caused by the Babine slide in one season, then extraordinary remedies will have to be taken to assist this year's run of salmon to get into the lakes so they can spawn.
I would ask the minister to be kind enough to give the committee information as to what has been done to date and what the expectations are for the immediate future in connection with this matter. While a rockslide may not sound like a matter of major importance, the complete blocking-and it was a complete blocking-of a whole run of salmon is a matter of major concern to the whole Pacific coast.

There is another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. Perhaps it is only fair to say that it should be given some consideration by the scientists of the department before any answer could be jxpected. This matter has been brought to my attention by the Prince Rupert fishermen's co-operative association. In passing I should like to say that in connection with these practical matters of local concern I doubt- I say this with great respect to all contrary opinion-whether there is any body better fitted to advise than the fishermen's co-operative association composed as it is of the men who do the actual fishing, who have day by day and year by year knowledge of local conditions and who because of the nature of their operation have a knowledge of the commercial end of the business as well.
This matter about which they are now making representations is that the department give serious consideration to the adoption of conservative measures in connection with flatfish. They have not made their submissions to me quite as general as that. What they have asked is that the department should be asked to take steps to ensure the closing of fishing in Skidegate inlet as soon as the flatfish taken in that area show evident signs of spawning. It was felt that this action was necessary in the interests of conservation.
I am not making my request in quite those narrow terms. I am asking the department to give consideration to investigating whether or not a situation has been developed where the conservation of flatfish should be undertaken. That may involve considerable inquiry, experimentation and research by the scientists available to the department. If this branch of the industry considers that we have reached a position where conservation is necessary, then I am quite confident in passing on that request to the department to make scientific inquiries into the matter. I feel that this matter would not have been brought to my attention by the co-operative unless they had cause to worry as to the future of flatfish.
There is another matter which I think is worthy of some consideration by this committee. In this particular instance the initiative on the coast is taken by the deep sea fishermen's federal union. I may say for the benefit of the committee that some two years agj the department operated on the Pacific coast a tuna patrol which was intended to investigate and report upon the movement of tuna. This was not in connection with conservation or spawning; it was simply an effort to find the crop available for fishing that year. That patrol was not carried out last year, and I understand no provision has been made for it this year. Evidently those 55704-204
Supply-Fisheries
engaged in fishing on the coast found that the tuna patrol was of real and practical value, and they have asked that it be reinstituted. I pass on their request with my endorsement. I realize that in the Department of Fisheries, as in all other departments, an effort must be made at reasonable economy, that we should not only conserve fish but should conserve money as well. However, if this tuna patrol is going to increase the catch of fish the amount necessary to keep it in operation will not be an expenditure; it will be an investment which would pay a good return.
I admit quite frankly that I am not in a position to state definitely that the industry will suffer if this tuna control is not reinstituted, but I am in position to say that the deep sea fishermen's federal union, which is a well managed organization, is of the opinion that it will. I submit these few suggestions to the Minister of Fisheries assuring him again, and I say this quite sincerely, that while we on the Pacific coast see fit to bring our problems to his attention that fact detracts not one iota from the appreciation we have for the way in which our interests have been looked after by him and his department.

Mr. Chairman, I had hoped the minister would make a statement. I have been reading again the report of the Department of Fisheries for 1950-51, and have found it a most interesting document. I had thought that if the minister spoke he would give us some information that would be appearing in the next report, which I suppose we shall not receive until several months have passed. It is to be regretted that the report of the department for the year just past does not come out until after the estimates have been considered. As a result hon. members have no opportunity of seeing what has been done by the department during the year.
This report indicates that a great deal of activity was carried on during 1950-51, and I imagine there has also been a great deal of activity during 1951-52. The minister was present in the chamber a few minutes ago when I spoke on the question of unemployment insurance for fishermen. I am aware of the difficulties to be encountered in connection with this, but I am sure the minister is also aware of the plight of many fishermen when there is a bad season, either because the catch has not been sufficient or the price has been low. He knows that in 1950 the price of salt codfish in Newfoundland was low. The officials of the fisheries prices support board were put to work on the problem, but they were some time in

Supply-Fisheries
coming to a decision. I appreciate that they had many difficulties to contend with because there are so many fishermen and so many dealers. All the books had to be examined, and each fisherman's account had to be inspected.
I would point out to the minister that the principle which was adopted was unsound. The principle followed by the fisheries prices support board upon which payments were based was to average the value of fish at $10.10 per quintal of 112 pounds, and then they averaged the price the fishermen were supposed to have received at $8.80. The difference of $1.30 per quintal was paid to all fishermen who had been selling shore fish.
I say this principle was unsound because some fishermen received higher prices than others. Those who sold their catch in August and September received the highest prices, while those who sold their fish in October and after that received very low prices. As I pointed out previously, some of them received an average of $5 to $5.50 per quintal, yet they received the same amount, $1.30. The minister must be aware, and certainly the officials in the fisheries prices support board are aware, that all fishermen did not receive the same price for their fish. It seems to me that where they are not catching sufficient fish, or because of bad weather they have not been able to take good fish and therefore will not get a good price, they are put in the position of men who are out of employment. Their income is low, so low that they will not be able to carry on for another six months until the new fishing season begins. It is the same for the fisherman as if he had been out of employment.
The Minister of Fisheries is aware of that problem, and I suggest that instead of giving a straight figure of $1.30 per quintal on the fish in 1950 a more elastic system should have been adopted. A higher figure should have been given to those who received the lower prices. If that principle had been adopted in 1951 I think he would have found a lot of people would have been entitled to receive some amount of money from the fisheries prices support board. What is that board for? It is supposed to help people in the post-war era. This is still post-war. The conditions that have existed in the European markets are certainly not nearly so good as they were in the period before the second world war. The export of salt codfish to the traditional markets in Europe has been affected by the war and conditions arising from the aftermath of war.
Therefore it seems to me that the fisheries prices support board should come to the rescue of fishermen when they receive low

prices or when they make poor catches. I should like the minister to keep the welfare of the fisherman directly before his mind. I have made this same appeal before. He can have all kinds of bait depots, longliners, drag-gers, cold storage, experimental kitchens and that sort of thing but that is not helping the fisherman directly, and it is direct assistance which is most appreciated.
I said a few minutes ago that the number of fishermen prosecuting the fisheries is declining. I do not know what the figures are for 1951-52 but I see from the figures in the report for 1950-51 that in 1949 there were 26,758 fishermen in Newfoundland and in 1950 there were only 22,556. That is a decline of over 4,000. How many were there in 1951, and how many will there be in 1952? The number of schooners taking part in 1949 was 232 and the number in 1950 was only 105, or less than half. I feel quite sure that the principal reason people are leaving the salt cod fishing industry is because of the uncertainty of the fishery, because the fishermen are not always able to earn a living wage and are not receiving insurance benefits which people receive who are out of employment.
I have here an item from the May 12 issue of one of the daily papers published in St. John's. The report is from Grand Bank which is one of the principal settlements on the southwest coast of Newfoundland, and is in the district of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. The article reads as follows:
The fishery continues good for the shoremen around here. The dories are getting a quintal and better daily. The catch is being salted now and will be sold undoubtedly saltbulk. It was encouraging to hear Mr. Lane express his confidence in an improved situation and price to be realized for this year's catch. He urged fishermen to remain in the fishery but this will not follow this season in some sections. We understand that in the Marys-town and Lamaline sections that a fairly large proportion of the trap fishermen do not intend to prosecute the fishery this year. In fact, some of them have burnt their bridges behind them and have sold their traps and skiffs.
That is only one section, and I believe the same is also true of other sections. Therefore I believe the problem should receive urgent attention on the part of the minister.
During the past week a question has been on the order paper in my name arising out of information that came to my attention. The hon. member for Charlotte had a question on the order paper a short time ago in which he inquired as to the amount of assistance that had been given to farmers under the Canadian farm loan board and the amount of assistance that had been given to fishermen under the fisheries loan board. I do not think the title he used with respect to the fisheries loan board was correct. It is a very long involved title. Its

short title is the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act. It is very enlightening to make a comparison and I think that was the object of the hon. member for Charlotte-between the assistance which has been given to the farmers of Canada and the assistance which has been given to fishermen by means of loans. Under the Canadian farm loan board the amount of assistance given is small in comparison with that which is given under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I urge the minister to give consideration to having the act relating to fishermen altered or to introduce a new act to provide that fishermen can take advantage of the same provisions which are now applicable in lending to farmers.
Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act a farmer may apply to a bank for a loan for anything to assist him in his business or anything to improve his home or surroundings in order to make life more pleasant in the home or to make his business more profitable. All he has to do is go to the bank, and if the bank thinks his credit is good it will give him a loan of up to $3,000 with seven years to pay and the government will guarantee the loan. Last year $85 million were loaned by the chartered banks of this country under that act. Since the legislation was passed a few years ago $255 million has been loaned by the banks, and the bad debts only amount to 1/100 of 1 per cent.
The hon. member for Charlotte asked the amount of money loaned to fishermen under the fishermen's loan act last year. Do you know how much it was, Mr. Chairman? It was $800 compared with $85 million loaned under the other method. It must be apparent to all persons in the house that similar provisions should be extended to fishermen as are extended to farmers. The hon. member for Charlotte urged that, and I support him. I have been in houses in Newfoundland, and perhaps the minister has been in them too, where there are industrious men who make a living but sometimes have a poor year. They do not feel justified in making a big expenditure for a boat, a new engine, a new trap or other useful objects that could help them in their business. A longliner, for instance, would cost a lot of money. I refer to things of that kind that would help him to improve his catch or improve the value of the catch when he is curing it.
On the other hand he might wish to have something in his home in order to make a better place in which to live so that his wife and family will be more comfortable and contented. Where is he going to borrow the money? Suppose he needs $1,000 to 55704-204J
Supply-Fisheries
instal an electric pump or a water or sewage system? Let us be frank and honest about this matter. Thousands of fishermen of Newfoundland have no such amenities at all, and nobody will lend them the money to put those things into their homes. If the minister wants the people of Newfoundland to remain in the fisheries-that is, those who are fishing-he must see to it that there are available to them advantages similar to those that are available to the farmers.
According to the latest census 55 per cent of the people of this country are now living in the cities and only 45 per cent are living in rural or fishing communities. The trend is away from rural communities, where there are so many disadvantages, into the cities .where they have the bright lights, the heated homes and all the modern conveniences. One of the objects of the minister with regard to the fishermen of Newfoundland should be to make their homes as comfortable as possible.
While I speak of the fishermen of Newfoundland I am thinking of the fishermen in the other provinces as well. This type of loan should be made available to all of them. If the minister does not feel he should do that, I assure him that at the earliest possible moment I propose to introduce a resolution- if I cannot introduce a bill-into the house asking the government to give consideration to this matter, in order to get a decision by the government upon it.
The Secretary of State is familiar with the fisheries of Newfoundland. Not long ago he made a statement about them. I do not know whether he did this on his own-probably he did-or whether he did it with the approval of the Minister of Fisheries, which was not necessary. His broadcast was favourably commented on in an editorial in the Evening Telegram published in St. John's, I think on April 26. The Secretary of State said:
It is only trash to talk about prosperity in Newfoundland until the fishermen are placed in a position to earn a good living according to present-day standards ... I cannot too often repeat that the two great problems are: to increase the catch of each fisherman, to improve the quality of his product so that it will fetch higher prices in wealthier markets.
I am aware that the Secretary of State has for a long time been an advocate of long-liners. His advocacy of this form of catching fish has been ridiculed by the provincial minister of fisheries in Newfoundland, but this newspaper seems to support the Secretary of State. A little while ago I put a question on the order paper in order to find out what was the cost of operating these longliners and what was the value of the catch they made; and I was surprised to find they were losing money. When the minister is on this

Supply-Fisheries
item, if he has any figures which were not available to him at that time I should like him to indicate, if he will be good enough to do so, whether the experiments that have been carried on in connection with the long-liner have been successful, whether further expenditure on that account is warranted, and whether that system of catching fish should be more generally practised in Newfoundland. The figures that were given in answer to the question I asked do not seem to me to justify the expenditure. However, there may be longliners and longliners. There may be boats that use long lines which are more suitable for the fisheries of Newfoundland than are others.
There is another matter about which the fishermen in my riding have spoken to me frequently and which I believe is generally considered by the fishermen of Newfoundland to be important in connection with catching fish. I refer to the supply of bait. The federal department of fisheries has a bait service. It has at least one steamer which goes around to the different settlements where no bait freezer is established and supplies bait to the fishermen; but there are still a great number of places to which this steamer does not go and in which no bait is readily available. As you look around the peninsula of Avalon through my riding, starting at St. John's and going south around Cape Race and up St. Mary's bay and into Placentia bay, how many bait depots will you find? There is one at Ferryland and there is one at St. Mary's. In St. Mary's bay there are a great many settlements where there are fishermen; in fact in all the settlements there are fishermen; and it is not a sufficient answer to say, "There is a bait depot over there", 15, 20 or 30 miles away. It seems to me there must be some way of having bait made more easily available than that.
In a letter which the minister wrote me I think he spoke about "holding depots". I do not know whether any holding depots have been built since I first brought the matter to his attention, but I do not know of any. I do not see any improvement in that situation since I first directed his attention to the matter. The fishermen are always talking about it. What it means is this. Trap fishing begins in June. It may last the month of June and go on for a couple of weeks in July. In most places it will be over by the end of July. In some places it may go on for another week or so. When trap fishing is over-that is catching fish by large traps-the fishermen go trawling or hand-lining and they must have fresh bait for those forms of fishing. It is necessary that it be fresh. The cod are very particular 
fish. They must have their bait fresh. If the fishermen have not fresh bait they cannot go fishing. Therefore as we get toward the end of the summer the fishermen find it more difficult all the time to go fishing because they cannot catch the bait to use and it is either too far to go or there is some other obstacle with regard to procuring bait from the bait depot.
In St. Mary's bay there is an island called Colinet island where all the men are fishermen. In fact in most of the settlements-St. Vincent's, St. Joseph's and North Harbour- practically all the able-bodied men are engaged in fishing. It is a good many miles from North Harbour over to St. Mary's, and it seems to me unreasonable to expect that a man should hire a truck and go around perhaps 30 or 40 miles and come back again -that is 80 miles-with bait and then have no place to keep it; or to go by boat, which would mean going 15 or 20 miles in a motorboat out into the open sea, which means great hardship for the fishermen; and he would not be ready to go fishing if he had gone that distance. I would therefore urge again that greater consideration be given to this question of bait depots, bait freezers or holding depots, whatever you choose to call them.
Two years ago last April fisheries development committees were set up in Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, each headed by the chief justice of that province. They have been sitting for two years. While I was not aware of the one in Prince Edward Island until recently, I was aware of the nature of the people on the committee in Newfoundland. It is a joint committee with federal and provincial representatives. They have sat now for over two years. I wonder whether the minister is in a position to give us any information as to what that committee has done, or whether it has made any interim report. The premier of Newfoundland has come out with some rather strong statements about the changes that must take place in the fisheries of Newfoundland and the large amounts of money that must be expended if they are to be put on a profitable basis. I wonder if the minister is in a position to make some remarks upon the statements made by the premier, or at least some statement on what the committee has been doing and when it is likely to furnish us with a report. Apparently a great deal depends upon the report of this commission. It is composed of able men, and they have been two years on the work. After two years I imagine they should produce something very beneficial to the fishermen of Newfoundland.
I notice that in the maritime provinces the Department of Fisheries, during the year

1950-51, set up a number of fish hatcheries. I do not think there is any fish hatchery in Newfoundland. Has the minister given any consideration to the building of fish hatcheries in Newfoundland? I would say it is most important that we should have fish hatcheries for lake trout and salmon. Many years ago the Newfoundland government brought out a Mr. Chambers from Scotland to investigate the salmon fishery. He made a report in which he recommended the establishment of a fish hatchery, but I do not think it was ever established. I should like to see one there, because in my opinion the quantity and size of the salmon caught in Newfoundland has declined over the years.
The salmon fishery is certainly not what it used to be. From the point of view of angling it is a remarkable attraction for tourists. We have a lot of fine rivers, but unfortunately the cutting of wood has interfered with the flow of water. We have had low water more often and more seriously of late years, and as a result the fish have died. Quite strict conservation measures, therefore, should be put into effect.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Does Newfoundland contemplate any reforestation measures on these watersheds?

I have to inform the hon. member that the Conservative party is not in office in that province. If we were in office there I believe we would take far better steps to see that these rivers were protected.
What I wanted to know is whether or not they are taking any measures.

I have been an advocate of reforestation for a long time, but recently the provincial government has termed the nursery where young trees were grown for the purpose of reforestation-well, they have used some opprobrious term.
This is Friday, Mr. Chairman, and I think we should stick to fish and not trees.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The minister points out that we are on the first item of the Department of Fisheries, and that we should discuss fish and not trees.

If the minister cannot see the connection between reforestation along the rivers and the salmon fishery he does not know very much about the salmon fishery of Newfoundland, because it is largely dependent upon having a good flow of water in the streams.
